A JUBILEE EPODE. Lady, God lends a torch to light Thy path to peace transcending dreams. Uphold it! See, from height f o height, Across the day, across the night, Its splendour streams! God gave the realm, God gives the light— How sweet, how bright, It beams !

; That torch is Love, Nt hose lucent ray Slays all things cruel and unclean! ;o shadow clouds it night or day, While sun and moon keep equal sway, Calm, and serene. : God gives this torch with heaven-fed ray To light thy way, 0 Queen! Let this thy guide and sceptre be, And power and peace may still be thine, I All mortal men shall bend the knee, , All:men revere, in thine and thee, The law divine. Blest shall thy mighty Empire be, r While o'er the world from sea to sea, The sunlight of thy Jubilee Shall shine! ...-Frotn the Contemporary.
ROBERT BUCHANAN:

A JUBILEE SONG. Upraise the song of Jubilee; • Rejoice with acclamation! From sea and shore, to shore and sea, In high and lowly station! • Give praise for homes and days serene, And sing, God bless our Gracious Queen— Our country and our nation! Through joys and sorrows smiles and tears, Love bath been her deferlder ; Her early vows, through fifty years -0_7•47.,, Have known no base surrender. 7 Her people's good bath been her own, Their trust the bulwark of her throne, Their love its highest splendour. For all the good her reign bath won, • Our grateful thanks are swelliug ; Great things for us our God have done, His mercy ill dispelling -Hath made in widely-sundered lands One brotherhood of hearts and hands, One race, in love excelling. Long may her gracious years increase, May brave and wise endeavour Make strong for progress and for peace— A kingdom none may sever: May love still win its noblest fame, And righteousness, in deed and name, Exalt our land for ever! —Sunday at Home.
MARY ROWLES.

. - PURE FRAGRANT ! Mr. F. MONKS, in r • espending said it was quite true, as , REFRESHING! had been saicf by Mr. Daviuts, that all their interests were For TOILET and NURSERY • ' bound up together, but of all the interesta in this country EXHIBITION HONOURS, there-was none that ,would ,compare with the agricultural Fifteen International Awards tor absolute Purity and absence of industry. When they thought of the enormous valow of the Artificial Colouring.' - produce of the soil of this country it dwarfed entirely half a dozen of the other big trades. They might take, for in- stance, his own trade—the iron trade—the cotton trade, the —Fear wthite Hands— coal trade, the woollen trade, and the silk trade, and roll Brie. t, Clear Cemptexioa them up together, and they did not auto ant in value to —suetifealthful Krim.— one-half of the value of the agricultural prodece of the PEARS' SOAP country. (Hear, hear.) After all the manufacturing trades Is spatially prepared ror the deli very largely depended on the agricultural trade. They were cite data ot ladies and children all interested in the land to that extent, and and others sensitive to the wee- thee, winter er summer. p"& there was one thing he might be 'excused for mentioning, vents ttednese, Roughness, and and that was that VA land lawe of this country Mapping. would have to overhauled before either manufacturers or agriculturiste could reap the full benefit of the soil. Not , only would they haver to'abrogate royalties, but the land- lords would have to Bee to it that they had duties to the • land as well as the farmer. He was pretty well satisfied; that after these land reforms had been made they would be ! able to meet the competition of the world, as Mr Davies had said. At present they. were handicapped in this coun- try in the iron trade to the extent of some as to Ns per ton by royalties, which he ventured to say no landlord ever ought to have possessed... That waxaquestionivitich would have to be settled by and by. (Hear, hear.) Referring to those stores he said he was quite sure—although he had not discussed the matter with any of his farming friends— that the farmers of that district had already found the ad- vantage of the establishment of the stores by being able to get more reasonable prices than they would have done if the stores had not been established. (Hear, hear) He looked forward to those stores being a great success, and bringing in a good return to tbe share- holders. He himself had had a part in start- ing the Co-operative Stores in Sankey-street, and he knew they had immense difficulty is steering that society throug.tidte early difficulties which mainly arose. front the members themselves, but judgment and patience enabled them to gat through all thoseinitial difficulties. He had no dotebt initial difficulties would also affect the Farmers' Stores, but he felt quite sure that with the practical good sense of their deputy-chairman and the business habits of their chairman and the directors associated with him they would be able to steer through all the difficulties that might present themselves, and that as a result the buyer would , be benefitted and they as sellers would reap better profits. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN WEIR next proposed the toast of the "Invited guests?' Alderman &mons, in responding, said he could assure them that the people of Warrington looked forward with ex- pectation to the future of that association. tie believed they had inaugurated a system that would be equally advan- ' tageous to the shareholders and to the town. (Hear, hear.) They might rely upon it that any facility that could be afforded them in the conducting of their business as business men, would be afforded them. (Hear, bear.) He hoped that as the town increased their customers would increase also, and he trusted it would be found that there , were no business men in the town who followed their bush- netts in the way they ought to do that would bre prejudiced by the soccess of these stores. He thought there was room for them and room for these who were here before. (Hear. hear.) Alderman Burgess concluded by expressing the hope that at the end of twelve months' time the Jure- i holders of :he associatii;n would have placed before them a ' faequrable statement of their affairs. (Applause.) Mr. MONIES next moved a vote of thanks to the chairman, which baying been paseed and acknowledged, the pruceed- ings concluded.

The arrival of Vincent Lorraine at Curramore was the most exciting, event that had occurred in the district since "98," and nobody talked of anything else, from grand Mrs. O'Conor, at Clanmorris House, to the herd boys and boOrotters. Rumour had long bestowed on the,Englishman an evil reputatiori, which, thanks to Terence O'Conor, though not to him alone, had been filled out with some; circumstantial details that gave to the picture. a very inky hue indeed. Naturally, in such a community, even those vices of a wealthy man of fashion which " Society " allows to be quite venial are regarded as all but unpardonable; and as Lorraine was looked upon even at the London clubs as very fast, the gentry of Gabiay had some cause to lift up their hands at the sound of his name. Still, lie was the possessor of immense wealth, unmarried, and, it appeared, remarkably handsome; so it is not to be wondered at that Ws. O'Conor began to cherish bene- volent intentions towards him, and to dream Of accom- plishing a reform of his character through the medium of pretty Dorine, her daughter, who knew all about Mr. Lorraine's English property, and would cheerfully undertake the reformation of its owner; or leave refor- mation alone, so long as her position was not injured by her husband's pursuits. Of course it speedily travelled to Clanmorris House that Hyacinth Desmond had met the lord of Curra- more the day after his arrival, and that the very next day she had walked with him from Grady's farm to Drumabog ; and Dorine tbonght that Hyacinth was getting old enough to behave more carefuliy, or else that her mother should look after her a little better. Doriire had spent two seasons in Dublin, and on the' strength of this experience regarded Hyacinth as an untamed country colt, who stood in sore need of in- struction. Still, the two had been very good Mends. Hyacinth, laughed at Dorine, and continued to ride her shaggy popy without a riding habit and often without the aid of a saddle, danced jigs on the shortest notice, and ran in and out among the cottages like a tame kitten; but it was not impossible that this friend- ship might be impaired if Hyacinth—whose beauty Dorine could not well deny or even underrate—should attract too much attention from Vincent Lorraine.

It chanced that nearly a week after the advent of the English landlord, Hyacinth rode up to Clanmorris House on Shetnni, and ran into .the drawing-room where Mrs. O'Conor and her daughter, the former gelded before her writing desk, intent on sending out invitations to a ball which, after much discussion, it, had been decided to give in ten days' time in honour Of Mr. Lorraine, whom neither of the ladies, it should be added; had as yet seen, .though Dorine had driven about in her little pony carriage in the hope of en- countering him. "Well, Hyacinth," said Mrs. O'Conor, a somewhat stately and handsome woman, kissing the girl's cheek, "I am glad to see you—we haven't had that pleasure for four days.' , r "Is it so long ?" said Hyacinth, turning to greet pretty, fair-haired Dorine. "I thought I would tell you the, news.; first, Mr. Lorraine has a beautiful horse, said he went all the way to Trahone himself k• fetch it, and rode it back—". "How do you know, that, Hyacinth?" asked Donne. "Am I not, all over the country? don't I know
every breathing thing within twenty miles round ? The horse came yesterday—Shaun Geohegan told me that—and I saw Mr. Lorraine on it as I came here/'

"You mean yOu spoke to Mtn?" Hyacinth shook her curly head. "No; I haven't spoken to him since I walked with him to Drumabog, —he was a long way off. My sec9nd piece of pews is this: Pat Doodan and Fergus Creagh have both had notice to quit—Mr. Lorrraino served.the notices with his own hand yesterday morning; and Fergus Creagh offered to pay the rent he had refused before, but Lor- • raine wouldn't take it.' He Said he wouldn't have such tenants." •

"He is mad`to act so," exclaimed Mrs. O'Conor ;•" it is playing bagatelle with his life." "Why, yes; and there is nobody at Curramore but himself and Margaret Finnigan—not a man about the place. He told Dan Murphy he didn't trust any of them, and so far he is right, and he wouldn't have any of his own servants over, because if anyone was to be shot one man was enough,' and that's a good trait in him. It would not be 4asy to break into Curramore ; but someone might manage to enter during the day, secretly, and hide himself." • "With Margaret's connivance?" "No ;,,Margaret would be faithful. I don't know what she thinkii,of this lord; but his father, you know, saved her son's life, and got him out to America, and she has always been grateful. Anyhow, Mr. Lorraine is fearfidly reckless." "And very odd," added Mrs. O'Conor. "He has not called on anyone; perhaps he despises 'native' gentry, or is too proud, imagining that we would not receive him on account of his character."

"'!ha that, Most likely," said Hyacinth, remembering how her mother had counselled her to see no more of Vincent Lorraine than she could help, and added that she (Mrs. Desmond) would ce4ainly not 'Offer him a welcome if her position had been different; as it was, he would not probably ask it of her. Mrs. Desmond- cared not a rush for wealth and status; good blood .and high character were all she valued. "Tracy says,' pursued Hyacinth', "that Lorraine 'broke the hank' at Monte Carlo two years ago, and won a lot of money at last year's Derby. I didn't know what breaking the bank was till Tracy explained it, and I wouldn't care to touch money won in that way or won by turf betting." ; • Dorine looked shocked: but said—

" Still, we can't altogether ostracise him, can we? and it is too late for us, at any rate, to do so. We are going to give a ball in ten days, Hyacinth. to celebrate Terry's return, you know, alid we have asked Mr. Lorraine." "You and your mother will come, I hope," added Mrs. O'Conor, hoping also—though she was too well bred even to imply this—that Mrs. Desmond would: decline, for Hyacinth always threw Dorine in the shade. "Thanks," said Hyacinth, who dearly loved dancing and society, "I know I should be delighted, and I am • sure mother Would too."
"You her, with my love, will yoc, dear? and, of course, you'll dress here, as usual. The ball is fixed for the —th." - .

Hyacinth stopped chatting a little longer, gave Dorine some 'Suggestions for her dress--for the girl had an ‘'etquisite taste—and then took her leave, ' mounted Shemus, and rode off. She had not ridden far on the common, which was nearly two miles in length, when she heard a quick hoof-stroke behind her, and thinking it might be Tracy Mansfield, drew rein and lookerbacked. It was not Tracy, but Vincent Lorraine, splendidly mounted on a dark bay horse, and riding with a perfect grace and ease that won Hyacinth's profound admiration, though she hardly knew whether she was vexed or pleased to see him. In a moment he had reached her side, and pulling up. bent down to her with out-stretched hand, and a glad light on his handsome face that left no doubt' of his pleasure at seeing her. "Well met," he said, with that rare sweet ,voice which had so strange a charm. "It seems an age since I saw you, Miss Desmond." - .

. , "It is only ra few days," said the girl, more reser- vedly, he thought, than she had spoken last time, and giving him her hand less frankly. "I thought it was Tracy coming." , " Yon would not have drawn rein for me, then ? " said Lorraine, with one of those keen, even bold, looks of his into the fake, at once so sweet/and so noble, that made his heart throb as it had never throbbed before for any woman, "but I could have easily caught you up, you know." "I should net have ridden away, Mr. Lorraine. You must think poorly of Irish manners," said Hyacinth, a little haughtily.

"I only je,sted —you know that," returned the young man, quickly. • "Have I really offended' you ?" "No," said Hyacinth, wishing he would not speak so earnestly about so small a thing, ariethinking of that affair at Monte Carlo and other escapades, too, she had heard of him ; and she put out her hand and patted the horse's neck, to create a diversion. Vincent Lor- raine looked down on the little \ delicate hand, as she had once looked at his, only with very different

OWD BETTY JIIBIbEEIN. Me un eawr rum has,bin Jublileein. rother d • way went th' Manchestur Eggshibitionrun aw'l tell I you heaw it is us way wer so beheend hond 1 obsarvin .t/i' Jubilee. Last wick eawr Turn wur readin papper Us heaw th'-poor foke had gin seven hundret theausand peands to th' Queen fur a Jubilee present. Aw sod its very gud o' foke fort help her a it neaw. Aw dassay hu'l a spent aw her bit o' brass i' buyin her cloos fur hersel un dowters, tin soords un hosses fur Prince Halbert un Prince Henry uv Butterbird, tut t'others us took part ith' Jubilee dot). They tell us heaw awt Queen's childer is eawt o' work, un a dassay its a job for her t' make eends meet un tee. If way'd nowt but thee workin" way shud Soonrbe flunnnuxed. Ger eawt,theaw gre,yt blunderbus, eawr Turn sed, quoit hot, dussant theaw no Us heaw th Queen has monny o' score o' theawsand peands gin her harey heear b' th' Parlement, un ut Parlement keeps uw her childer besides.. Hu hoos Mester Parlement, aw sed. He favvurs havirk a gotd deol o' brass, un bein verry free with it. Aw think aivst roite Misses Palrlement un ax her send her mon to Goburn. By sew, hees that sort a mon, he'd stir Goburn up. If Mester Parlement, or sum other mom us has brass un_as a, moind t' spend sum on't dussant le comm n afoor lung, one hauve o'th' foke Goburn ul havt gut Becko Lone. It favvurs to me us awt foke us cared abeawt Goburn, un cud do a bit o' summat fur it, has oather deed or flit; un its quoite toime way leet sumbry no as there is sich a place. Fire, un empty bellies. bike th' bayles, has cum beawt sendin fur, un if way wanton sumbry t' fill eawr bellies un shunt th' bayles wast I hay' t' send for um, aw'm shoor. Aye, Bet, eawr Tum sed.

Shut up, a sed, thay'n bin tryin'. a greyt whoile t' regilate Goburn, un a foine mess thay'n made on it. It favvurs time us if they'd dun Goburn same us Doctor Trostus, sowd it to owd Sam. - Aw back adverti4n. They advertize i' th' papers abeawt soothiesirrup, 1211 stuff •for makin' wiskers, un whoi shuddent wey advertize Goburn, and let sum- bry no wheer it is, un heaw it is? If sirrup im wisker*chaps didn't let foke no, foke wud noather be suthed nor ha' wiskers, un if way dunnot adver- tize for sumbry wi brass to corn an' tak care on us west hay' t' go t' workheawse. ''' That's aw 6 Hast dun, eawr Turn sed. Eigh, aw sed. Well, he said, theaw'rt biggest owd bledderyed 'us ever aw coom across. Theaw'rt bike a deol mpor wimmiji IGoburn ; when tha tang gets waggin', its bike ehexpress enjun goin' deawn nil hincloin ;it connot stop if it kilt onybody. Best plan is t' keep eawt P th' rode, for tburs dangiF when your on th' . track. Theaw geet upo' rung loin, un istid o' goin' , north tha's gon south, and lost thissel awegether, un me very neer. Aw wer tell& thee abeawt Par- lement keepin t' Queen un her childer. Eigh, aw 1 ses, theaw anus' nose it aw, goo on. Parlement is a lot o' foke elected fro' different places, same us way 1 I elecon Meeter Lee for here. tin, aw ses, what Par- lement un not dun, they pretend t' do. Its i Len- non, he said, un they makin laws un taxes. Hest ' never heerd owd Bottlecock. ravin' abeawt his lysens brass, un owd Towser swearin' abeawt th' hincome tax. Eigh, aw sed. Well, Parlement makes thoos. ' Beside thoos, they collec'n havvpen- nies un pennies fro' t' ir or foke, un when they'n paid th' Queen un her childer, they divide rest amung theirsela un other foke. tin heaw much dust think Queen has. had awfgether, aw as. Monny a hundert thousand peawnds, un neaw her hardly nose what hu's woth. Tother day there wer a clark i' -won o' th' banks, i' Lunnon, wheer t' Queen puts her brass, ancl, he happent oppen th' book us shows heaw much hu has in. He were sacked theer un then. It favours fro' that us if thayre feert o' lettin' foke no its that much. ' Neaw, aw ses, to eawr Tura, howd on, aw con see very well as thes a suprise i' store fort poor foke i' this counlry. Hu's bin howdedback for th' Jubilee. Th' Queen knows very weel heaw win bin plaked. Hu nose as heaw work has bin sears un meight hard be getten. Hu nose as theausands o' poor childer has wanted butties an cuddent get um. Th, bitter cry o' want has bin loud un hu man a heerd it. While &NV this has.hen goin' on hn's never mist a meal's meight, nor had one thing less upo' table. If th' country's bin poor theyn not dropt her wages, an her an' her childerlas bin seen wed l to. Neaw ha ses hu'l ciim eawt hansom. Poor foke ul get summat neaw just to celebrate th' Jubilee wi', an' wen way getten eawrs wayl goo to th' Eggsbibition at Manchester. Eawr Turn harkent eawt, un he spent monny a heawr aside o' Waumsleys fort' see if he cud beer owt. He thowt o' goin' th' Liberal Club, but sumbody town him as he didn't need goa . theer, onybody us loiks Oirish, they said, ud nare' ha nowt fro't' Queen. They towd him as heaw th Pimrosers met do summat, but fort' ger amung hum he'd hav't' have a regalcy—un he'd nowt reet color but his red flannin shirt, un that ud bin patched. He cud heer nowt, goo wheer he wud, an at last aw persuaded him t' go un ax Mester Saaiilson if he'd heerd owt abeawt th' Queen's bounty. He towd eawr Turn as heaw th' Queen had gin nowt. Hu had, he sed, axed the Lord tak care o' aw her sub- jecs, but as for hersel' hu cud doo nowt fur hum. Eigh, eawr Turn sed, that's a verry general and cheop rode o' gettin rid o' poor foke. Aw wonder heaw it would be, he sed, if way stopt tap whoile toimes are bad, un recommended th' queen and th' royal family to th' same sours: If hu'd only gen th' brass us poor foke has gin her or a hospitul or a workheawse it wud a looked better; but fort goa un spend it upa' a moniment as they sen hu's gomt do is a caushon. Whoi, hu's not spent us mich upo' Jubilee us hu did upo' a moniment forJolinDreawn ; but hu happen thinks us heaw vvast do beawt kings and queens i this country, soon an has saven up so as her childer con keep thersels. Eawr Turn was quoite upset, and aw said, nere mind, us aw hay getten three hauve creawns us aw've saved up for they nu shoon. Way'l goa wi' that and Jubilee at eawr own hexpens. So way geet us reddy an went t' Manchester, an next wick;avel tell yoa aw abeawt wot way seed an heerd. 1

"I may say he is a be'a.uty, though I am his owner," he said smiling. "Damian is a good friend, though be is not my dearest. I did not care to have him over, to be, perhaps, shot. How is your little patient,, Biddy?" "Worse ; it is a sort of low fever she has, but think she will turn the corner. I hope so." "I should have thought the hope would pi the other way," said Lorraine. "Children go straight to Heaven when they dir, don't they ?" "Yes ; but their mothers prefer kwping them," re- plied Hyacinth. "Even when they cannot provide them with shoes? or, perhaps, shoes are considered as pure luxuries. Still, if you are fond of Biddy, or think, on principle, that she ought to be kept alive, and to that end needs what her parents cannot give her, pray draw on me." Hyacinth looked up wonderingly. If be meant what he said he put it in the oddest manner, as if Biddy wore a kitten or a bird, about whose existence he could not be expected to care anything, one way or the other, for its own sake or the sake of humanity; but if she (Hyacinth) had a weakness for the creature, he would do what he could to preserve its life. She could not thank him for succour offered in such a man- ner, even if be meant it; it was a piece of careless galanterie, she thought, for Hyacinth was not vain enough to perceive a deeper feeling, and would not have felt flattered by it if she had. "I daresay," she said, "the Gradys can give Biddy all she needs. They are not really poor, as you know. fihe would be umier no obligation to him if she could help it, so he read her answer, and he was partly right. He bit his lips, lint said quietly— "I am a sad cyniC, Miss Desmond. I wish I could imbibe some humanitarianism ; but I am sinner enough without adding hypocrisy to the category. My motive is good enough for me, though you are too good to value it; but Biddy would not regard motives, so long as she had what they procured, and you would perhaps, forgive, would you not?" Adamant could hardly have resisted the tone and manner of that appeal, and Hyacinth Desmond was a sensitive, passionate girl, without an ounce of adamant in her composition ; so she lifted to the young manis face those large, clear eyes
Whose glances, deep with April tints of sunny tears,

had power over him she little wist of, and answered gently, and a little archly-- "I would not have anything to forgive, I suppose; hut if I had, then I would forgive it, because of Biddy." "I wish—l will say it, at the risk of incurring your displeasure—that you may have to forgive me, 'because of Biddy,' though I know you do not."

- Hyacinth coloured, but laughed. "I never like asking favours, Mr. Lorraine." "You are hard on me, Miss Desmond. I asked you to confer a favour." " That is the orthodox way of putting it, isn't it ?" said Hyacinth, lightly. " Mr. Lorraine, I must push on, for I have two or three places to go to before I turn homewards."

" One moment's grace," said Lorraine, laying a de- taining hanf on her bridle, "there is a question I must ask: Shall you be at Mrs. O'Conor's ? She has honoured me with an invitation. Of course yon are. asked?"

"Yes," said Hyacinth. "I have just come from Clanmorris, and they have asked my mother and my- self; but it depends on her whether we go or not." " But it really rests with you, does it not? Then you will go ?" "I daresay---I cannot tell," said Hyacinth, con- fusedly, trembling, and shrinking back, and half-in- clined to hope that Mrs. Desmond would refuse the invitation.
"I shall expect to'meet you," said Lorraine, bending down to her, " and you will give me two dances at the least."

'Oh, I could not make any promises," said the girl, hastily. "Please loose Shemus, Mr. Lorraine; I must indeed go on." He did not seem to heed the touch of peremptoriness in her tone. He obeyed at once, with a low spoken " Pardon !" but only to take the right hand she scarcely offered, and hold it—for the first time—with a close pressure that made her heart leap up with a sharp pang of blended anger and dread, and something that was neither one nor the other, but held her passive in a, strange subservience to his will. "You will promise," he-said, softly, not in question hut assertion; and again she felt, and flushed under the gaze she would not meet: It was in a kind of bewilder ment that she answered—

. "Yes," and hardly remembered afterwards whether she had given an affirmative answer or not, or whether she had intended to do so. Lorraine said nothing in Words, but bent his lips to the little hand, and kissed it as no man should kiss a woman's band who feels ,no mOre than the impulse that prompts a mere courtly .galanterie, and then he released her. For half a mile after she left Vincent Lorraine's side Hyacinth did not know what way she went, and if Shemus had not known the road as well as she did herself, he might easily have gone quite astray without check or hindrance from his young mistress. Even when her mind grew clearer, her only definite feeling was of passionate indignation with Lorraine, which made her decide one point about which there had been hitherto some uncertainty, and decide it against the Englishman. She thoroughly disliked him, she said to herself, setting her teeth as she said it ; and .vet, despite her just anger, she seemed to imagine her- -elf in some sort bound by a promise not fairly extracted ; and presently, as she rode onwards, a dan- gerous light grew into the girl's eyes---the first dawning, of the women's knowledge of her power to give blow for blow, stab for stab. Such men as Vincent Lor- raine would always find amusement wherever they were; he thought, no doubt, to

"—Break a country heart, For pastime ere he went to town;" lie must work some evil, or he would die of ennui ; and it was a sort of amusement especially congenial to him to make somebody in love with him, and enjoy the pleasure of flirtation, the while he laughed to himself at the ease with which he won affection he did not return. He, doubtless, thought himself irre- sistible ; and she (Hyacinth) was beautiful, she knew ; at any rate, everyone told her so. And Vincent Lorraine had not been careful to hide front her what he thought on that point; so she was to be the butterfly he would catch in his net this time. He should learn for once in his life of selfish profligacy that defeat was possible--even for him, and if seeking to wound, or only playing with edged weapons in the wantonness of long impunity, he should, perchance, in his turn be wounded, verily, it would be well for him. Bitter thoughts for one so young; but surely Vincent Lorraine was far from being guiltless, if he should reap pain to himself. He had scarcely so lived as to have any right to be surprised if his attentions were held to express no more than a passing fancy ; and it was not a fault, but a virtue, in Hyacinth Des- mond—in no man's thoughts more than in his own— that she so utterly underrated her own power to make or mar a man's life. It would be a grim retribution for the worse than waste of so many golden years if the very purity and guilelessness that won' the man's homage should deal hint the most deadly wound he had ever know n—a wound that no time could soften, no physician heal. (To be continued.)

The man who stirs his cup with an icicle spoils the tea and chills his own fingers. Life is a sacred trust to all. He is derelict who does not take due care of his own; he is guilty who does not respect the lives of others. A lady lately accounted for the sudden arrival of her son from Cambridge by explaining that he "had ridden all the way on his encycloptedia." A schoolmaster, describing a money lender, says "He serves you in the present tense, he lends you in the con- ditional mood, keeps you in the subjunctive, and ruins you in the future." Judge every man by what he cannot do, and you will find no man of ability. Judge every man by what he has accomplished in the fields with which he is familiar, and you get at his real size. Cabby: "Beg parding, mum, but I don't think I've a pocket big enough to put 'ern in . .

John Burns was tried at the Glasgow Circuit Court, on Wednesday, for shooting his mother-in-law and wounding another woman. A verdict of culpable homicide was re- turmd, and Lord Adam sentenced the convict to fifteen Years' Penal servitude. The high road to success has never been a smooth or even course. One must be prepared for a perplexed and tortuous path, and many apparent failures before the goal is reached. He who turns back at the first obstacle will certainly never achieve his end. At Rochdale. on Wednesday nichto a greengrocer named Thomas Brierley, who was Buffering from the effects of heavy drinking, cut his throat with a knife, and also tried to throw his son, six years of age, from an upper window. By the prompt action of some nolice officers the lad was rescued, and Brierley, who struggled desperately, was taken to the Infirmary. It is hardly likely that he will recover.

Xettero to the .Maitor. THE JUBILEE FESTIVITIES AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—l was favoured with your Saturday's issue and supplement, and had great pleasure in reading such a glow- ing account of your loyal Jubilee festivities. Especially was I pleased to read of Mr. Alderman Crosfield's liberality, and of our venerable townsman, Mr. Beamoct, being present. thought a line or two, informing you that we also in Ains. dale commemorated the Jubilee of her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen would not be out of place. We have in our midst at Ainsdale an,old Warringtonian, who remem- bers the Jubilee of George the Third. He was born on Friars Green, Warrington, and received part of his early education at the day school connected with the Blue Coat School. His name is Thomas Woodward. His father worked for Mr. Edward Greenall at Wilderspool, but re- moved to Chester, taking his family with him. He is very hale and hearty, living with a married daughter, and was selected to carry, at the head of the procession, a portrait of her Most Gracious Majesty. He will be 89 shortly. The name of the schoolmaster at that time was a Mr. Bullock; he was a cripple, or lame of his feet. If Mr. Wooaward should ever visit Warrington, perhaps Mr. Beamont would like to see him to compare notes.—Yours truly,
C. ilowcocx. Lancaster-road, Ainsdale, June 30th1 1887.

THE LAST JUBILEE. Sir,—Sitting here in my " owd arm cheer," not a hundred miles front " Slutcher's Lone," of blessed memory, lam try- ing to make out which of all the schemes for the Jubilee com- memoration was the best. Right or wrong, I have come to the conclusion ihat "pulling down the wall" was the choicest. When I saw that some of my dear old cronies had hit upon this idea, I was simply delighted. It was grand, it was magnificent, it w‘,3 jolly ! A "Jubilee hearse," "new cemetqy," or a "fresh police van" were nothing to it; and the misguided individuals who would have sub- stituted a "Free Library" deserved laughing out of existence. What! the common herd to read those books for which they pay taxes! And may be to soil or " thumb " them, so that their " betters' " fingers should be in danger of contamination! Perish the thought! When will these short-sighted artisans and others see what is best for them? Their blindness gets more apparent every day, and their bumptiousness more so I Suppose they did get the Free Library—what would be the result? We should have some moonstruck beggar pitching upon the "Immortal '4 il- liatri'9" works, and going about in the last agonies of "King Lear," or "Macbeth," and thee, farewell to those inimitable quotations so plentifully, and yet so judiciously, interspersed through the brilliant orations of a late mayor. From any o' her lips, would they be worth listening to? I trow not! No ! no! n Free Library! As one of the idealists said to pie : "You see, if we knock a wall down, that wall will never get up again. It is, therefore, an act in perpetuity; but if you build a wall, or a van, or a hearse, or a cemetery, they must, sooner or later, come down; and then posterity will miss what we meant for them." This reasoning put the finishing touch to my doubts; and I could as soon question the wisdom of Solomon as that of my old fellow townsmen who were first struck with that scheme. l's a inarey We've got folks to tell us The rghts and the wrongs o' these matters I vow— God sends e iuntry josklns, and other wise fellers, To start a gremd scheme. when it gitsis a slough And "our Joseph," says he • WI II —no, never I—agree To give Ignorant persons a library free I" -
Amen! OLIVER TWIST. " Sloteher's Lone," June 29, 1887.

LOOK AT BRIDGE-STREET. Sir,—l see from your report of the proceedings of the Town Council thal a shy and somewhat diffident attempt is to le made to remove the wall opposite the Town Ball. I don't ask that our sapient Councillors should, for once in their experience as " men of light and leading," be bold, because 1 rather think that now the majority have got a chance to clear away the wall, the Conservative Club is not likely to have it as an eyesore much longer. No. I would rather give them some little encuragement to go boldly into other matters which require their immediate and care- ful attention.

I suppose, sir, it is no use my stating that a little bold- ness on the part of those, whom I see one of your contem- p.,ries calls " mere nobodies," would have given us, long ere this, a Free Library. I should scarcely gain credence for such a statement. Very likely I should be reminded of the great necessity there is for care and economy; do nothing rash, and so on. Well, I may leave the library question ; perhaps November will be a more suitable time for ven- tilating it. But, if care and economy are to be special at- tributes of the occupants of a council chamber, what shall we say of Bridge-street? Does the naked and desolate ap- pearanc., of Bridge-stret reflect, creditably, upon the wis- dom, or foresight, of our c•nincillors ? I think not. I wish to ask, sir—and I know many of our townsmen would like the question answering as soon as possible,—how long is it to continue? If it is a:fact that the ratepayers are losing a thousand pounds a year, the sooner Bridge-street is re- built the better.

I have heard it said, more than once, that we are in the unfortunate position of being without one single indepen- dent town councillor. If this be an untruth, may I suggest that some member ask for and insist upon receiving a clear and full statement of the whole of the expenditure incurred in buying land and buildings in Bridge-street, together with I details of sums paid to lawyers and surveyors? Farther, that a sketch be given of the calculations by which it was hoped the town would reimburse itself for the outlay entered into when the scheme for widening Bridge-street was first projected. I believe something like £29,000 has been ex- ; vended as purchase money solely. At a calculation of £3 per yard, the returns may be £1.8,500. There is a margin of considerable breadth floating somewhere. Will the borough treasurer give some help to elucidate the mystery, or is it all a myth? If the suggestion I now put is not heeded, I shall, most reluctantly, believe some of the things I am told, amongst them being one to the effect that the various committees are little more than "rings," to get into I which is difficult; to remain in impossible, should a man I display any sturdy independence. I can understand a reluctance on the part of gentlemen , to sell the land at a loss, but if reasonable bids are made, as 'I have re tson to think has been the case more than once, it is folly to hope that the success of the Ship Canal scheme will recoup the losses incurred by refusing such bids. I am strongly of opinion that the tradesmen and residents of Bridge-street hold views upon this question that would be all the better for a little ventilation. Tradesmen, to do a satisfactory business, seek a popular and attractive thor- oughfare. I ask—ls Bridge-street attractive? Certainl7 not. People coming into town will make at once for the centre, and thence will spread in all directions, save one, Bridge-street.

Sr' long as the people are willing to live under the old and pernicious system of individual ownership of land, they must abide by its results; one of its results is to be seen in Bridge-street. Exorbitant sums of money have been ex- ploited out of ratepayers' pockets into the pockets, largely, of men who contribute nothing whatever to the productive•resources of the town, with the added injury to Ps bona.fids trade. If the Councillors can stoop low enough to hear my whis- perings, I would further add that it might be better to make the first loss on the transaction the last. The best way to remedy the bad business would be to set fairly and earnestly to work to sell the land, satisfied with such a price as would enable purchasers to conduct a trade on legitimate lines. WA prices for land mean high rents; together they mean high prices for goods, with the result of driving would-he customers to the stalls of the itinerant dealers, and then we bear vicious discussions on Free Trade. If I am not mis- taken, the records of the Council will prove that warnings as to what was likely to happen were uttered years ago by Mr. T. U. Rylauds, but, as we now see, to little effect.

CHAMBERLAIN AND HOME RULE. wonder when we are to have an end of the base misrepresentations that are from time to time, and with such rapidity, being written by the Gladstooian section of the Liberal party, first towards Mr. Bright and then Mr. Chamberlain. Is there to be no end to this sort of thing, or is misrepresentation towards our public men to be the most important doctrine in our Liberal creed? Simply because such men as Mr. Chamberlain differ from Mr. Glad- stone's ill-emened scheme for the better government of Ire- land, be, forsooth, is to be manufactured Into an inconsis- tent Radical ; and what beats all is that your correspondent "Fiat Justitia," should have the courage to quote Mr. Chamberlain's speech in the Warrington Public Hall in support of his attempt t prove the inconsistency of Mr. Chamberlain. It is quite true that Mr. Chamberlain in the Public Hall spoke of our Liberalism as being broad enough to include within its borders all the friends of progress to settle our own differences, and Mr. Chamberlain thinks so still. And who is it that has been the means of prevent- ing the Irish question from being settled amongst ourselves but Mr. Gladstone? Who of the Liberal leaders (put aside altogether the country) were consulted with regard to Mr. Gladstone's ill-considered plan in trying to force upon the party his Irish measures, based upon principles that were well known to him to be in direct opposition to the pledged opinions of Mr. Chamberlain and his other col- leagues? Mr. Chamberlain, before accepting any office in Mr. Gladstone's last government, on account of the rumours that Mr. Gladstone was entertaining a scheme for giving Ireland a statutory parliament, took great care to put be- fore Mr. Gladstone his opinions on the Irish question, and he was consoled with the promise that it was only his intention to have an inquiry into the question. COMP' " Flat-Justitia," and tell 118 where was the inquiry which Mr. Gladstone promised, and which beguiled Mr. Chamberlain into the Government under false pretences? I want to know if " Fiat-Justitia," or any other man in Warrington, believes in his heart that Mr. Chamberlain advocated in his speech in the Public Hall the principle of a statutory Parliament with full executive powers? It is well known that just before Mr. Chamber- lain came to Warrington, Mr. Parnell put a sort of mani- festo before the Irish people, which was to this effect. That, in his opinion, the time had come to abandon alto- gether ail attempts to obtain further remedial measures, or subsidiary reforms,and to concentrate the efforts of the Irish representatives upon the securinu of a separate and —mark you—independent Parliament, whose first object it would be to put a protrctiye duty against all English manufacteres. The MSC was proved by Mr. and Mrs. Stuart., of St. Helens, who saw the offence committed in the Wigan Market Hall whilst making pur- chases. This they reported in the local press, and the Royal Society took it up. The defence was a complete denial—The Bench considered the case proved, and fined the defendant 20s. and costs. £5OO OFFERED FOR A TICkET TO WESTMINSTER ABBEY. —Dr. Parker, preaching in the City Temple on Sunday, said he had been astonished at the interest taken in the Queen by their American friends. He could have sold his Abbey ticket for £lOO to an American; indeed, one American had offered as much as £5OO for a ticket. The Americans have no Queen, but theybad education, liberty, independence of spirit, the spirit of progress, and invin- cible energy. It was, however, right of them to recognise that within the past fifty years England had bad cause to rejoice that there was such a woman on the throne. INTERESTING DISCOVERY AT WINCHESTER CATHEDRAL. —At Winchester Cathedral on Thursday, in preparing a place for the stone inscribed with the name of Edmund, eldest son of Bing Alfred, the receptacle of the heart of Bishop Nicholas of Ely, 1279, was uncovered, and was carefully examined by the Dean. In a. block of stone, protected by a plate of lead and an upper slab of grey marble, was found the case containing the heart The case, which was presumed to be of pewter, was sewn up In a napkin of silk or damask. The vessel was not un- covered, and was carefully re-interred, alter Mr. Bargent. the antiquary, had taken drawings. Bishop Nicholas of Ely was Lord Chancellor and Lord High Treasurer of England before be became Bishop of Winchester. THE FRATRICIDE AT LIVERPOOL.—The young man John Golding, who killed his brother, Martin Golding, a dock labourer, aged 32, at 31, Sterne-street, Liverpool, on the night of the 18th inst., was brought up at the Police- court, on Monday, on remand. The evidence was that the prisoner and his brother were playing cards with a man named Roberts. The trothers, who were under the influence of drink, quarrelled, and Martin called John a ?cheat, and struck him. The prisoner secured a butcher's knife, which was lying on the table, and some time after- wards stabbed his brother with it in the left breast. The knife cut through one of the ribs and went thraugh the ' body to the back. The injured man was removed to the !Royal Infirmary, but died in about an hour afterwards. —The prisoner stated that after the quarrel his brother ent out for some drink, and he (prisoner) got some of , and remembered uothing after that.—U% was corn- -sitted for trial on the capital charge. _ _ FATAL ACCIDEICT TO AN EICCIHSIONTST AT WTGAN.—On Monday night an inquest was held at Wigan on the body of Benjamin Marks, who resided at Mount-street, Brad- ford, and was a driver in the employ of the Great Northern Railway Company. On Saturday morning the deceased, In his capacity as a railway servant got several passes, and With one of them he travelled Wigan. Here he left the train, but on its movingiout of the station he made a rush for a second-class coanpart- ment. He put his left arm "aside the carriage, and with the right hand, in which he held a stick, he attempted to open the door. This he succeeded in doing, although frequent calls were made to him from the platform to desist. When the train had gone about half-a-dozen yards he was knocked back by the door, and fell between the carriage and the platform. He was crushed into an almost shapeless mass. An independent witness gave evidence that there was no fault attaching to the railway employes, and the jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS..
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS..
THE' 'EGYPTIAN CONVENTION.-` OPPOSI- TION TO ENGLAND AND TURKEY.

RERUN, fdormar Ninny.-- The course of events .in Constantinople is naturally followed here With great interest. The following statement regarding the situa- tion is from a first-rate source :—" The central Powers, Germany, Austria, and Italy do nbt- wish for a confer- ence on the convention .regarding which they remain neutral except, that Germany has endeavoured to influence Russia. with which Power she is again on ex- cellent terms, in favour of the convention. Even if her efforts prove vain a conflict is not feared. The French Government is decidedly pacific and shrinks from a conflict with England, despite its oppo- sition to tli-- convention. The Czar also ;c at present thoroughly licaceful, and wishes to avoid t•ly outbreak. Even if the apparent agreement of Russia and France in opposing the convention continue they are far from in- tending combined action, so that all will remain as it is If the convention be not sanctioned by the Powers, Above ali it will be necessary for England to evacuate Egypt. On thecontrary, her position there is essentially strengthened by her rapprochement to the Sultan, whereby his secret action against the English oectipa- tion of Egypt comes to an end. The main question for England in this case is to satisfy the Sultan's financial claims, and then his opposition will be at an end."

THE AFGHAN UESTI ON. —RUSSIA'S - • ATTITUDE. SIMLA, MONDAY.—Frorri information received here, it is believed that-the Ghilzai rising against the Ameer of Afghanistan is collapsing. a large number of insurgents are returning to their homes. ODFISSA, MONDAT.—The South Russian press thinks, that the Afghan question contains the germs of ugly com- plications for England which may rapidly develop. The labours of the mixed commission are afßrmed to be Very trifling, and concerned only with side issues that are liable any day to disappear under the magnitude of the general question. Either England or Russia, or both will be compelled;the writer thinks, shortly to interfere for the pacification of the border kbanates. This kind of advocacy on the part of the Russian press is very significant.

div.head: LETTER FROM _THE QUEEN'.
div.p: LETTER FROM _THE QUEEN'.

A supplement to the Landau Gazette was issued on Saturday 'evening containing the following letter, re- ceived by the Secretary of State for the Heine Depart- ment from the Queen Windsor Castle,lune ga, 1887. "I am anxious to express to my people ,tray, warm thanks for the kid, and more than kind, reception I met with on going toiand returning from Westminster Abbey. with all my children and grandchildren. • "The enthusiastic reception I met with then, as well as on all these eyentful days. in Londom as well as in Windsor, on the occasion of my Jubilee. hae touched me most deeply. It has shown that the labour and anxiety of 50 long years, 22 of which 1 spent in unclouded happi- Deis, shared and cheered by my beloved husband, while/ an equal number were full of sorrow and trial, borne without his sheltering arm and wise help, have been ap- preciated by my people. “This feeling and the sense of duty towards my dear country and.supjects, who are so inseparably bound up with my life, will encourage me in my task, often a very difficult and arduous one, during the remainder of my lite. .
-- - "The wonderful order preserved on this occasion, and the good behaviour of the enormous multitUdes as- sembled, merit my highest admiration.
"Thai God nsa-y srotect and abundantly bless my. country is my fervent prayer. -
"VICTORIA R. AND I."

The Dean of Westminster states that, after paying all expenses, there remains as the proceeds from the service held in Westminster Abbey on Wednesday last the sum of £2,500 to be divided among the London hospitals. The number of persons present was - . tal to that of the previous day, and reached nearly 1000.

div.head: GREAT FIRE IN•NEW ZEALAND.
div.p: GREAT FIRE IN•NEW ZEALAND.
WELLINGTON, WEDNESDI.T..—A great fire has occurred at Blenheim, destroying an hotel. a bank, and twenty-two shops. The low is estimated at £50,000.
Baron Hirsch has forwarded a donation of £lO,OOO towards the fund for the establishment and maintenance of the Imperial Institute.

div.head: nib; SHIP CANAL- INQUIRY.
div.p: nib; SHIP CANAL- INQUIRY.

, In the Douse of Commons, on Monday night, the Ship Canal Bill was, on the motion of Sir W. H. Honlds- worth, read a third time.—Mr. Childers reported on the bill from the Committee as follows :—That the bill does not authorise the construction of any new works. The object of the bill is to enable the Manchester Ship Canal Company to raise a portion of their authorised capital by the issue of preference shares. That, in pursuance of the order of the House of the 14th June, the Committee has heard the opponents of the bill, namely the Mersey Docks and Harbour hoard, the Corporation of Liverpool, and the London and North-Western Railway Company, on the question' of the effect upon the said opponents of the -alteration of the financial conditions imposed by "The Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885," so far as the said opponents were protected by the said conditions, and has also heard witnesses on behalf of the promoters. Oct Committee, after hearing the evidence and con- sidering the circumstances of the case, are of opinion that -the powers sought by that bill should be granted, Subject to provision being made in sub-section 40, 'clause 2, that £2 per share shall be paid up on the ,£3,000,000 to be issued as ordinary shares, and to a pro- vision that not more than £6 shall be called up on any ,preference share until a like amount shall have been ,called up on each ordinary share, and vice versa. That there are no other circumstances of which, in the opinion ,of the Committee, it is desirable that the [louse should be informed. Mr. Childers further reported from the Committee that they had examined the allegations of the bill and found the same to be true, and gone through the bill and made amendments thereunto.

The Manchester Ship Canal (Preference Shares) Bill having been introclaced in the House of Lords on Monday evening came before the Examiners for that HOU93 on Tuesday on proof of standing orders. As the statwory no- tices bad not been given, the Examiners were obliged to decide that compliance with • the standing orders had not been proved. The promoters will therefore have to take their case before the Standing Orders Committee. It meets on Friday. The Parliamentary Committee of the Liverpool Corpora- tion held a meeting on Tuesday, Sir W. B. Forwood in the chair. to take into consideration the present position of Liverpool as regards the Manchester Ship Canal, and the re- cent decision of the Comeuttee of the House of Commons in favonr of the application of the directors of the canal to be allowed to issue four millions of preference stook. After discussion it woe unanimously resolved to petition the House of Lords against the powers sought for, which if allowed will practically reverse previous decisions of the House of Commons, and it was decided to engage Mr. Pope, Q.C., to advocate Liverpool interests before the House of Lords Committee.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

On Thursday night some bailiffs, strongly protected by a large constabulary force, and in possession of . ten head of cattle, were attacked by a large mob, who stoned the police and bailiffs and attempted to rescue the cattle. The police charged and dispersed the crowd an impounded the cattle. Three young men were drowned while bathing in a small inlet ot Lough Mask, at Clonbur, on Sunday. They could MI swim, but one of them became panic-stricken, and on the others gging trs his aid they were all drowned. One of the deceased, named Murray, leaves a widowed mother and several young children. The Central News is enabled to state that the five honours conferred last week upon Irish efficials does not at all exhaust the list of Irish Jubilee honours, and that several knighthoods and other titular distinctions will be conferred, but the announcement of the intended recipi- ents will not be made until after the Royal visit.

Three men, named Murphy, Bradley, and Mc.Sorley, were at the .Belfast Police Court, onldonday, sentenced respectively to three, two, and one month's hard labour, for rioting in the Falls district on Saturday night, when the police were compelled to use their revolvers. Five shots were fired, and one man, who was carried off by fellow-rioters, was woundede, Brown, the militiaman, whose arrest for drunkenness caused the disturbance, was to-day sent to gaol for two months. A correspondent having inquired from Mr. Justin M'Carthy, M.P., whether the statements concerning the health of Mr. Parnell were correct, and whether the hon. gentleman was about to retire from the leadership of the Irish Parliamentary party, Mr. M'Carthy replied : "There is not the slightest truth in any report which asserts that Mr. Parnell is about to retire from public life. The Irish party have never talked of or thought of electing any other leader in his place. We all hope to see him very soon restored to perfect health."

Mr. Parnell, having been called on to arbitrate between Mr. Sexton and Mr. Gill as to who should be Lord Mayor of Dublin, writes to Mr. Gill: "I greatly regret that anit member of the Parliamentary party should be placed in a position of antagonism to one of his colleagues, and I think it would conduce to harmony in our ranks if you could see your way to reconsider your decision in accept- ing the nomination." Mr. Gill has accordingly requested the Lord Mayor to convene a meeting of the Nationalist party in the Corporation, to accept us resignation and select a successor.

On Saturday, at Dundalk, Mr.llan, coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Anne Hughes, of Rock Mars4all, end her newly-born childien. On Thursday mornihg the girl arose at day- break and went out to herd a cow in a field about 150 yards from the house. About 830 "a.m, she returned and went to bed, complaining of being unwell. She ate her breakfast, dinner, and supper, but after the latter meal she grew worse, and on some of the neighbours being called in _thy discovered that the girl had beeLaifind.,_ Shirdied soon afteivitas, and on saiWbeing Made the bodies of two newly-born infants were found ift the, field. The jury found that the girl died from the effects of having been Confined flu. assisted together with the exertion of walking so far afterwards; and that the children died from want of care after birth.

Archbishop Walsh writes denyinghaving remonstrated against 'Monsignor Persico's mission, which the Sove- reign Pontiff, influenced not only by wise reasons but by that special feeling of affection towards Ireland and her people, recently decided upon sending to Ireland, and adds that, knowing what he does of the nature of the projected mission, and the object it was intended to accomplish, no thought could be further from, his mind than that of offering any remonstrance on the subject.

div.head: DROUGHT.
div.p: THE DROUGHT.

In consequence of the drought another mill was stopped at Accrington on Monday morning. Unless rain falls more mills and wdrkshops in East Lancashire will have to be stopped this week. Rain has only fallen on two occasions during the past week. Owing to the drought, the Blackrod Local Board, which daily supplies Horwich with 58,000 gallons of Water, has informed the Horwich Local Board that they are now about to reduce the supply -by 8,000 gallons Per day, which supply will only be available from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. On Saturday, Messrs. Geo. Knowles and Sons, Nv. 2 Peel Mill, Bolton, stopped for lack of water consequent on the drought. In many cases the mill lodges are very low, and very soon, under present circumstances, fur- ther stoppages will have to be reported. It is satisfac- tory to note that the town's .supply is abundant for week's to come., In consequence of the drought, the Stockport Water- works Co.; on Monday morning, announced that an intermittent supply must be given unless great economy be exercised in using the water by the inhabitants. For 21 years the rainfall has not been so low at Lyme, the supply district for Stockport. Such is the scarcity of water at Swansea that it is being sold in the streets at a penny per can. In some districts the inhabitants have had no water for two days. The weather shows no.sign of breaking, and the greatest alarm is felt. What-makes the matter worse is that what. water there is now in the reservoirs is very thick, and unfit to•drink. The protracted drought in South Wales is causing much anxiety to the local authorities. The reservoirs supplying Llanelly are nearly empty, and owners of works have been warned that, unless rain falls within a feW ' days, the 'supply of water will have to be cut o'ff. Slibuld this step ha-de to be resorted to, nearly 5,000 operatives will be thrown oui of employment.

Steamers which have brought cattle aeroes the Atlantic within the last few weeks report a serious loss during the voyage. The steamer City of Lincoln is reported to have lost about a hundred head of cattle.' She was bringing a large number of live stock from Montreal, and by the time She reached Quebec about, seventy of the animals were dead. The steamer reached Quebec on the 9th instant, and the carcases of the .beasts were thrown overboard. The steamer lost a fur- ' ther number during the Dosage across the Atlantic. It is believed that the heat was the cause of the heavy mortality. The steamer Bennington also lost a number of cattle in the same manner. Dunng the voyage across) 'the Bonnineton threw overboard about 56 of the car-1, cases, and on arrival at Liverpool she had several dead beasts on board.

Most of us must . now plead guilty to feeling warm, and we exchange meteorological remarks of an ungrate- ful character. What is more to the point, however, is that we should be on our guard against sunstroke, or, more scientifically, against insolation of heat apoplexy. Already cases of a fatal lurid have occurred within the rest few days, and Mall C' more, especially children of ten- .- years, have been Mu,. or less overcome. Gradually we come to understand that not the head only, but be neck requires to be protected against the danger. it is less generally realised that sunstroke_ may be pro- duced without direct exposure to the rays of the sun. A close room, exhausting labour, want of ventilation, irregular food, heavy clothing—all these are contributory causes to prostration by heat. It goes also without say- ing that stimulants are bad for those who have to work hard under the present conditions 'of temperature. Cold bathing and exercise in the cool Of the evening are good preventive measures. Flannel should be worn next the skin to prevent sudden chills, and the dress should be of a colour that does not readily absorb heat.

div.head: SAD DEATH oN THE CRICKET
div.p: SAD DEATH oN THE CRICKET

_ FIELD. • A melancholy incident occurred during the pro- gress of a cricket match between the Norley and Winnington Clubs in Winnington Park, on Saturday afternoon. The Norley team went in first to bat, and two wickets fell for 14 runs. Mr. W. Hayes • was third man in, and he was soon joined by his , brother, Mr. Sohn Orison Hayes, of Gorstage Hall , near Weaver Lam. The last-named gentleman had ' not been at the wickets long before he,was seized with a fainting fit, and play was suspended. A wet cloth was applied to his head, and in a few minutes he rallied. ' His friends endeavoured to persuade him to withdraw from the match, but he said he felt well enough to reSume play, and did so. Mr. Woodhouse, of Norley, undertaking to get his runs for him. In this way he scored six points—three 2's—and hit vigorously at the last bal I of the over. The next moment he staggered, and , asked Mr. Baker, wicket keeper, to support him. He ; fell into Mr. Baker's arms, and was carried under the shadow of the trees, the heat being excessive. Here ; his friends did all they possibly could for him, but he never spoke. Dr. Joynson, of Northwich, who ; was informed of the occurrence by Mr. Wells on Winnington Hill, hastened to the park, and after a . careful examination pronounced Mr. J. U. Hayes t• .be dead; indeed, he expressed the opinion that he j expired almost immediately after the second seizure j The body was then placed in Messrs. Brunner, Mond J and Co's. ambulance carriage, and conveyed to Gos- tage Hall, where the deceased, who was married about two years ago. bad not long resided. He was within ten days of his 32nd birthday, and was the son of Mr. W. Hayes, of Runcorn and Ashttin Hayes. near Frodsham, a well-known proprietor of salt works in the Marston district. The sad event ' created a painful sensation in Winnington, and es- pecially in the neighbourhood of Gostage, where the 'late Mr. Hayes was very popular. It seems that he was known to be suffering from a weak heart, and the tropical heat of Saturday, combined with the excitement of the match, no doubt affected its action. Dr. Joynson having certified that Cardiac syncope was the cause of death, Mr. Churton, the coroner, did not deem it necessary to hold an in- quest. The funeral was fixed for Tuesday at Frodsham

div.head: • CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: • CURRENT POLITICS.

Mr. Parnell has removed his town residence in Brock- ley. Ile finds it necessary that he should live more in the country, and he is to be seen walking almost every day. He is described as a strong man broken and emaciated almost to a skeleton.

We wish, says the Banner, that we could confirm the sanguine utterance of Truth in reference to Mr. Beres- ford-Hope's recovery; but we regret to learn that, although his convalescence is reassuring, there is but little probability of his return to public life.

The chairman of a recent Liberal Unionist meeting at Leeds has received a letter from Lord Salisbury, in which he says" it is matter of very great gratification to receive :filch assurances of confidence in and approval of the present. policy of the Goverment from the representatives of so many schools of political opinion." The question of an autumn session still hangs in the balance, and it is believed that the Government, if pos- sible, will content themselves with asking Parliament to sit pretty late into Aug'Ust. •If this be so, and the Government persevere with the bill to confer on a com- mission ef Irish judges the right to try prisoners charged with certain aggravated offences, it may be taken for granted that ne bill of any importance not at present before Parliament will be carried this session.

When the Perpetual Pensions Committee re-assemble, the details asked for in reference to the case of the Duke of Richmond wRI be handed in by the Treasury, and the Cominittee will proceed at once with the consideration of their report Mr. Bradlaugh will probably submit a draft report, condemning the principle of perpetual pen- sions, and recommending that all perpetual pensions should be determined by compulsory commutation, the Treasury in making such commutation to consider the circumstances of the origin of the pension, and whether real service was rendered by the original recipient The Committee will also probably be asked to report that the rate of commutation of 27 years' purchase, usually fol- lowed, is too high, andothat the commutation of certain pensions appears to have been effected without inquiry into the merits of formal objections lodged with the Treasury against such course. The draft report will also probably make special mention of the annual sum paid to the Duchy of Cornwall. '

There are now six vacancies in the Parliamentary re- presentation, four arising from the elevation of mem- bers of the House of Commons to the peerage, one from succession to the peerage, and the sixth from death. In the Spalding division of Lincolnshire—the late member, the Hon. M. E. G. Finch-Batton, having .succeeded to the Earldom of Winchilsea—Admiral Tryon is the Con- servative candidate, and Mr. Halley Stewart the Glad- stonian. For the St. Ives Division of Cornwall—Sir John St. Aubyn having been created a peer—Mr. T. B. Bolitho has come forward as the Liberal Unionist candi- date, but no Gladstonian is yet announced. A contest IA in progress at Coventry, the' late member. F Mr. if. W. Eaton, having been raised to the peerage& His son, Colonel Eaton. has been selected in the Con- servative interest, and he is being opposed by Mr. Walter Ballantine on behalf of the Glanstotiians. Vacancies occur also in the Basingstoke Division of Hampshire and in the Hornsey Division of Middlesex, Mr. Sclater-Booth and Eil? James M‘Garel Hogg having been made peers. Mr. J. Blundell Maple Is spoken of as the probable Conservative candidate for Hornsey, Y'd no opposition has appeared. The death of Mr. ' Lionel Cohen creates a vacancy in North Paddington. Mr. Chamberlain. in a letter to the "Times," says he is sorry that Sir George Trevelyan, having now changed his opinions, should single out for iritter insinuation the friend and fellow-worker whom be chose only a short time ago to be witness to hia unshaken fid.lity and courage. Mr. Cham- berlain complains that Sir George has entirely misrepre- sented the meaning of certain passages in Ha speech to the Literal Union, and asserts Clot the Round Table Conference broke down upon Mr. Gladstone refusing to say whether he accepted or refuted the conditions which were proposed in relation to the amendment of the Home Riile Bill.

LORD HARTINGTON AT BLACICEORtf.—L,nt Hartington, M.P , speaking at a Liberal Unionist demonstration held on Saturday at Blackburn, said the object of Liberal Unionist Associations would be to help to rturn at the next general elect ion,whenever it came, candidates representing their own shade of Liberal opinions, and, in any ease where that may be impossible, to establish an organisation "to which Liberal Unionist opinion in the constituency will rally, and which will give its votes, its assistance, and its support to that candidate which will most closely approximate " to their opinions on what they coned 'ered to be the rust im- portant question of the day. He coidd Dot Ray whether the formation of a National party, of which there had been Some talk lately, was only a dream which was being in- dulged in by some people, or whether it was des- tined soon to become a reality; but of this he was quite sere, that the formation of such a party would not be re- tarded, on the contrary it would be accelerated, by the formation and by the energetic Drosecotien of Littera I Unionist Associations. Commentirg upon Mr. Gladstone's re- Cent utterances as to the propriety of extending the principle of Home Rule to other parts of the kingdom besides Ireland , Lord Hartington said he believed the solution of the pro- blem could only be found in the maintenance of one Ina penal Parliament with full control over the affairs of every portion bf the United Kingdom—A resolution expressing approval of Lord Haltington's conduct is opposing Mr Gladstone's Home Rule measures for Ireland was passed by a large majority. •
SIR GEORGE TREVELYAN AND MR. CHAMBERLAIN.

Sir Geo. Trevelyan has addressed an important letter to Mr. Halley Stewart on the Irish difficulty and the present position of the Liberal party. Sir George refers to the efforts made at the Round Table Conference tor reconciliation, and Mr. Chamberlain's speech on June 14, in which the right hon. gentleman mentioned the two Irish bills of the late Government having been finally abandoned, and spoke with satisfaction of the Liberal Unionists having been instrumental in knocking the bottom out of them. Sir George says he will not attempt to describe his feelings when reading the language in which Mr. Chamberlain taunts the other party in that Round Table Confer- ence with having made the concessions for which they asked. About the meaning; of Mr. Cham- berlain's la.uguage there could be no mistake 'whatever. It meant that Mr. Gladstone was to make changes in the details of his Irish policy which, if he had made a twelvemonth ago, would then have secured the support of Mr. Chamberlain and of the majority of the Liberal members who voted against the bill. But their advances had not been met, and one allegation made is that oldt party lines are disappearing, and that if there is to be a union it had better be a union with the Conservatives. Sir George, however, points out that much remains yet for a united Liberal party to accomplish—the Welsh diseStablishment question, regula- tion of the liquor traffic, the reformation of the Rouse of Lords, the municipal organisation of the metro- . polls, &c. Prom dealing with these abuses the Conservatives are restrained by their sympathies, their electoral interests, and their honest belief. Another allegation made was that the Liberals had behaved so badly of late that the Liberal Unionists could have nothing to say to them. To this he replied that it was the very worst recipe for mending the con- duct of the Liberal party to leave its ranks. The Liberal Unionists could not kill the Liberal party: but by withdrawing from it their influence and their moderating counsels, they might turn it into more extreme ccuries than it had followed in the past. Sir George then declares that the Liberal Unionists are ready enough to detect the mote in Liberal eyps, but cannot discern the beam in the Conservatives, Who had turned upon the Irish representatives, with whom tliey were formerly in close alliance, and treated them, not as Parliamentary colleagues but as enemies. Lord Ifartington desired to settle the Irish question in concert with the Conservative party, as the reform question was loWed ; but in that case they must leave no stone un- turned to send good Liberals to Parliament, or they 'would not get a very satisfactory Irish settlement. When this bill . be- comes law, any Irish editor who ven- tures to pen such a leader as we are now writing will be liable to be sent to gaol for six months. It will be ruled that he is inci- ting to the terror of Her Majesty's subjects, and he will be got rid of accordingly. We trust there will be many writers who will break the law.

Who would be free himself must strike the blow. As Mr. GLADSTONE finely observed in the noble protest which he made on Monday night The condition of the laws under which Irishmen live will be virtually affected by the discretion of the Executive. That is a tremendous fact. Our pride and our joy and our satisfaction as a free people has been that we live under the law and not under the discretion of the Executive--(loud Oppo- sition cheers)—and that has been the reason why Parliament has fixed periods for the existence of such exceptional laws, and deprived the Executive I of its discretion, and re-established a safe rule a law. But all this is disregarded by the " Constitu- tional " party; and the PRIME MINISTER is prostituting himself in order to be kept in office by the Liberal Unionists. He said, less that two years since, that coercion in Ireland would create ten times as much evil as it would repress. He was right—he spoke truly; but what shall we say of him now when he sets to work to create this ten-fold mis- chief P No language is too •strong to de- , nounce his turpitude. He will go down to posterity as the politician who thrust a sword between Englishmen and Irishmen when they were inclined to embrace each other as brothers, and the Hartingtons and Chamber- I lains will go with him.

THE sudden death of Mr. J. N. HAYES, whilst playing at cricket in Winnington Park, on Saturday, is one of those singularly tragic events which immediately bring to mind the phrase that "in the midst of life we are in death." The peculiar circumstances of the case suggest various reflections which are worthy of consideration. Cricket, notwith- standing the popularity of football at the pre- sent time, many be regarded as the favourite national pastime; and it has so much to re- - commend it that no one can have a word to , say against it. if played under ordinary con- , ditions. But the conditions are not ordinary when the heat is tropical as it was on Satur- day last, and it would be well if captains would take the lesson of this fatalay to heart, with a view to declining play in hot weather. Football is a winter game, because, from the violent exertion which it involves, it is recognised that it would be Altogether too trying for summer time. But it sometimes , happens that the game is not played in winter, even when an important match has been previously arranged; for the ground may be so hard with frost that a contest would. ,be dangerous to life and limb Common sense prevails, and the match is postponed to a more suitable day. And why should it not be the same with cricket? Why play when, , through intense heat, the conditions are un- favourable? We know it will be said that the case of Mr. HAYES was an exctptional one; he had a weak heart, and it will be urged that the chances are that if he had been fairly strong he would have suffered no in- jury through taking his part in the game. The case was indeed exceptional, and everybody must feel that it is a pity—a thousand pities —that Mr. HAYES did not take the hint I which nature gave, and retire from the field ! after fainting in the first instance. No doubt , he felt that the reputation of the team was at stake; he was anxious that there should be no less through failure on his part.. So he returned to the wicket and played until he was again seized with faintness, and instantly expired. And this brings us to another point, and that is that irreparably in- i jurymay be done to the body throne' overtion in hot weather without their being any outward , and visible sign of mischief. Who shall say that the young gentleman who lost his life on the cricket field on Saturday was the only one in the team whose heart was weak? or that a first enlargement of the valves of that all-ioaportant organ will not in one cricketer or another date from that day? Certain it is that if a physician were called upon to suggest some kind of action which would be likely to lead to valvular disease of the • heart, he could not do better than prescribe ! cricket or football in hot weather. The glory of a young man is his strength, and I if strength is a glory, it is worth preserving; I but this is not done by over-exertion under bad conditions. It is the pace which kills, ; and when the thermometer gets above 70, it is equivalent to the pace being considerably accelerated. There are young men to day who are constantly over-taxing themselves, in sheer ignorance of the harm they are doing, and who are thus laying the foundations of prolonged illness -and permanent disease. When the nation gets wiser. it -will insist on I our school children learning something about their bodies, as well as of their parts of speech. A knowledge of verbs and adverbs is a poor exchange for hypertrophy of the heart. Mean- time, it is advisable for officials of Cricket Clubs to consider whether it would not be better to make matches subject to the weather I —the understanding being that 'hot weather as well as, wet weather shall be a good reason for declining to play.
