SIR GEORGE TREVELYAN has addressed a letter to Mr HALLEY STEWART, the Liberal candidate for Spalding, which should be studied alike by Liberals and Liberal Union- ists. It is a temperate. clear, and convincing exposition of the state of pollllca4 parties, and of the duty, at the present time, of all who call themselves Liberals. Coming from a politician of the experience and high char- acter of the ex-Secretary for Ireland, who has sacrificed so much in advocating his views as a Liberal Unionist, the letter cannot but have weight with the thousands of Liberal electors who have, like him, hesitated for a time as to the right course to take at this crisis in the affairs of the nation. We could not but ex- press ourselves warmly the other day at the' audacity of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in reproach- ing Mr. GLADSTONE with giving way on the question of Home Rule; and it would seem that Sir GEORGE has felt strongly on this point, for he says:— I shall not attempt to describe the feelings with which I, who went as Mr. Chamberlain's colleague into a friendly conference for the purpose of obtain- ing certain concessions, have read the language in which he taunts the other party in that con- ference with having made the concessions f 3r which we asked. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN IS just now in the unhappy position of not knowing what he wants. He talks about knocking the bottom out of Home Rule, but he forgets, and some of his follow- ers forget, that he has stvlrd himself a Home Ruler. At Sheffield, in 1874., he said— " Irishmen had a right to govern themselves and their own affairs, and he was willing to

concede it to them." INlat more, we would ask, does Mr. GLADSTONE say? But further, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. on the 19th June, 1826, said I have always been a Home Ruler." It is self-stultifying to boast, after using language of this kind, that the- bottom is being knocked out of Home Rule; and we cannot wonder that Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN has felt strongly on the subject. After show- ing how unwise it is for the Liberal Uionists to ally themselves with the Tories, Sir GEORGE adds:—

The Liberal Unionists are quick to detect the mote in the eyes of Liberals, but cannot discern the ' beam in the eyes of the Conservatives. The Con- servative method of treating Irish questions and Irishmen has been wrong in substance and manner alike. They have deliberately, and for party pur- poses, entered on a course of furious denunciation of the representatives of the Irish people On account of events which occurred years ago, before the time when some leading Conservatives were in close alliance with those very Irish representatives, and when all of them were silently and gratefully accepting their political assistance. Having in 1885 refused to strengthen the law in order to deal with actual criminals, they now introduced cruel and terrible penalties which may be used against poli- ticians, and Press-writers, and they place these penalties in the hands of an Irish Executive con- taining Ministers who signalised themselves by their approval and defence of the most dangerous manifestation of Orange violence which has taken place in our time. Another quotation and we have done : The essence of Liberalism is that people should •be induced to vote by appeals to their-reason, and not by social pressure .and considerations of their personal interest. There never was a moment in our day when a greater force than now of social temptations and social penalties was exerted in order to prevail on men of all ranks and classes to leave Liberalism in the lurch. When Liberalism is fashionable there are always plenty of Liberals, but true respect is in the long run paid to those who stand by the cause in its hour of difficulty. J Let Mr. CHAMBERLAIN ponder on this, and I' ponder, too, on the fact. that there is not— and all honour to them—a single representa- tive of labour within the Unionist ranks. He has deserted the democracy, and he will find that the democracy have lost faith in him..

Sir Wilfrid Lawson has given notice to move, on the first suitable opportunity, "that an humble address be presented to her Majesty praying that when her Majesty con- fers any title or honours on any of her sub- jects she will be graciously pleased to state, in the same manner as is done when the Victoria Cross is conferred, the public services in respect to which such titles or honours have been bestowed." It is stated that the announcement was received with laughter and cheers. We can understand he "cheers," but why " laughter ?" Is it very ludicrous to imagine a connection, in some cases, between public services and honours ? If so, the more need for reform.

Mr. F. H. O'Donnell, late M.P. for Dun- garvon, is about to sue the "Times" for libelling him in the articles on " Parnellism and Crime." The "Times' has for a long time been trying to catch a Tartar, and hav- ing caught one it is to be hoped it will be happy, though we have our doubts on the. subject.

Mr. O'Donnell gives the "Times" a week to adopt the following alternative :—" i. Ex- plicit retractation of the libel, and sincere apo- logies to me, and my former colleagues. 2. Explicit and humble apology to the public opinion of England, which you have endeav- oured to envenom for the purpose of setting people against people. and nation against nation ; and 3. As a material confirmation of these retractations and apologies, and as a partial compensation for your horrible prac- tices against Christian and civic charity and fellowship, payment of the sum of Lio,ooo for charitable objects within the metropolis of London without distinction of religious denominations. This (Mr. O'Donnell says in conclusiDn) is my reply to your insulting challenge for explanations. You will have ample opportunity for letting me know what you think of it before twelve good citizens of London. Perhaps you will allow me to intimate a suspicion, finally, that you may be found to be as well disposed to shirk trial by jury as investigation by Parliament." Well done Mr. O'Donnell ! That is a good start; keep it up.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances when they first find their eyesight fail- ing, they purchase all kinds of inferior manufactured spec- tacles which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, Manchester, and 143, Lord-street, Southport, has inVented bis" Perfection " Spectacles, which he adopts at either of the above addresses at 7s Eid per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to he equalled in the country for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve the eight " free on application —Advt. APPOINTMENT OF BANK MANAGER AT RUNCORN.—We have pleasure in announcing that Mr. J. B. Holland has been appointed manager cf the Runcorn Branch of ['err's Bank, in place of the late Mr. E. A. Chorlton. Mr. Holland has occupied the position of sub-manager for several years, and his promotion will give general satisfaction. ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN COMMISSIONER.—Mr. William Hankinsen, mineral water manufacturer, and a member of the Board of Commissioners met with an accident on Mon- day. In alighting from a vehicle be fell to the ground, and ohs of the wheels passed over one of his arms. Fortunately no bones were broken. The injuries were attended to by Dr. McDougall. MEASLES AT WIDNES.—In consequence of the preva- lence of measles in tiimms Cross and Warrington-road dis- tricts, the Board Schools which are known by these respec- tive titles have been closed during the past week. The Board School at West Bank was opened as usu al on Monday morning as the disease has now become almost extinct in that neighbourhood where it fi,st originated._

Vim-Torts To BLACKPOOL should stay at the Station Tern- perance Hotel, right opposite Central station. Central position. Commodious and accommodating. Terms easy. —Apply J. Heap.—Adut. UNITED METHODIST FREE entracu, WIDNES. tin Sunday the anniversary cervices in behalf of the school, took place in the chdpel, and Mr. J. Bramwell, of Liverpool, preached to large congregations. In the afternoon Mr. J. Brough, of Warrington, delivered an address to parents, teachers, and scholars. On Monday evening an enjoyable entertainment was given by the scholars. Mr. R. Wright presiding. The collections realised upwards of £24. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES.— The annual sermons in aid of this school were preached in the chapel on Sunday by the Hey R. J. Ward, of St. Helens. There was a good attendance at both morning 'and everCng service. In the afternoon a service of song entitled " The great teacher," was given by the choir and scholars. Mr. S. Lamb was tb,. conductor, and Mr. J. Jones presided at the harmonium. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P,„ of Penketb, read the narrative, and Mr. H. W. Deacon, J.P., cccopied the chair. The collections amounted to upwards of £l2.

ACCIDENT AT A WIDNICS CHEMICAL WORILS.—At the works of Messrs. Goldioe, Davies, and Co.. chemical manu- facturers, on Monday. Patrick Buckley, a labourer, who re- Piles in West Rank-street, was seriously injured. He was on a pl,,tfarrn 30 feet high assisting to move some heavy pitch Pine logs, when his right arm became jambed between two of them. and a piece of flesh was torn completely off, exposing the sinews anti muscles of the limb. Luckily he did not miss his footing, or he might have been pre- cipitated to the ground. Dr. Richards attended to the man's injuries. BR/3Rsonct WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCaoor., RtnaconN.— The anniversary .'49 celebrated on tiuuday last, when the Rev. J. Williams Botcher, of Liverpool, preached two set- moos in St. Pod's Chapel. There was a good attendance at the morning service, anti in the evening the sacred edifice was crowded. A service was also held on Monday evening, when the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Charles Garrett. There was again a large congregation. On each occasion speciany-eelected hymns were sung. The collections amounted to £5O. of which £l7 was taken in the morning, £2O in the evening, sod the remainder on Monday evening. TREAT TO SCHOLARS AT ErITTON.—Hv the kindness of the congregation attending St. Michael's Church, Ditton, and other ladies and gentlemen, the scholars attending the schools were on Saturday afternoon given a treat as a cele- bration of the Queen's Jubilee. About 500 met at the schools, and marched, headed by a brass hand front Widnes, to a field kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. Longton. 4 Ditchfield Ball. Tea was provided, followed by a good programme of sports. Afterwards there were balloon ascents and gamrs.of various kinds. and at night a vAtarl display of firewwka was given. The Rev. C. W. WWI (vicar) and Mr. Lewis and others worked hard towards the suecess of the treat.

JUBILEE CELEBRATION kT DurroN —Yesterday week Dutton was en fete on the occasion .f the Jubilee demon- stration, given through the liueralßy of Mrs. J. Campkin and a few friends, in the picturesque grounds of Dutton Hall. The proceedings commenced 137 the children of the Board School haying a sail on the river, after which a binntiful meat tea was provided. '[he Frodsham Brass Band was engaged for the occasion, and rendered a good selection of dance and other music. Sports were indulged in, and priz,s given to the succesful competitors by Mr. J. Campkin. Before partin_t each child was presented with a thank entitled "The Life of the Queen," also a haa and a Plentiful supply of sweets and nuts. The grand old hall was thrown open for the occasion, and this was taken ad- vantage of by great numbers. Mr. and Mrs. Campkin would like to thank those ladies and gentlemen who so kindly helped them, and an math, their Jubilee demonstration such a great success. . _ _

§EItIOUS LARKING AT HALE.—Blfore Mr. T. Sutton Tim- mis, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Percy Padfield, a respectably-dressed croon.; min, son of a Liverpool school- master, was, charged with having, on tha 20th June, dove grievous bodily harm to a middle-aged mm named John Chorley, bricklayer. of Tarbock. From be evidence it ap- peared that Padfield is apprenticed to Mr. William Turton, of Burnt Mill Farm, Hale, and Chorley bad been employed at the same place. Os the afternoon of Monday, the 2011, Edward Tuiton, a youth. found Chorlev drunk and asleep in a closet on the farm. Failing to awaken him he told a number of his fellow labourers, and a suggestion was made ley one of them that Chorlev should be smoked out. The prisoner obiaired a handful of straw, which he set alight and then placed under the seat. In half an hour several persons went to see how Chorley was, and he was etill drunk and unable to stand. It was not noticed that he was burned. —P.C. 8.11, of Tarbock, said he saw Chorley in bed on Friday. He was suffering from severe burns, and was to() ill to attend court that day. Ho afterwards took Padfield into custody, and the prisoner, in r-pl v to the charge. said "Yes, I did. But what I did was in lark for the nnrowe of gottiog him off the closet. I had no intention whatever of doing him any hartn."—lnspector Keighloy said he had re- ceived a telephonic message from Dr. Brindle, of Pre•Pcot, who said it would be two or three weeks before Choi-ley would be able to appear, and if he went on well he could not attend court for a fortnight—The prisoner was then re- manded until July 4th, hot as allowed out on bail on his owo rectwlieances of £5O and two eureties.ef £25.

REWARD FOR BRAVERY AT RONCORE.—Mr. ThOmas Roach, clogger, of Fox-street, Runcorn, has this week been presented by the Humane Society With a silver medal and a certificate of merit in recognition of his bravery in saving a girl from drowning in the Bridgewater Canal on the 2nd of May. ILLTREATING A HORSE.—At Widnes Petty Session's, OD Thursday, Joseph Griffiths was charged with cruelly iii- treating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state. P.C. Davy. stated that about half-past eight on the morning of the 21st Jane, the defendant was in charge of is horse draw- ing a cart loaded' with stones. On the shoulders udder the collar were two raw wounds, about an inch and a half square. The horse belonged to the defendant's father. A fine of lOs and costs, or 14 days' was imposed. FOUND DROWNED AT WESTON POlNT—About half-past seven yesterday morning, William Smith, captain of the steam packet Queen of the Merrier. picked up the dead body of a man unknown in the Mersey at Weston Point. The body was naked, and was apparently that of a man 30 years of age. He had dark hair, no whiskers, but a slight moustache, and he had two blue " dots" on his left arm. In height be was about sft. Pin. The body seemed to have been in the water about 14 days. and now lies at the mor- tuary awaiting an inquest. Rungonw Boum. SOARD.—A meeting of ratepayers was held on Thursday evening in :Bethesda Schoolroom for the phrpose Of electing three members to the Burial Board. The Vicar (the Rev. A. Maitland Wood) presided. The re- tiring members were Messrs. James Handley, J.P.,'Richard Morris and George Moss, who were all eligible for re-elec- tion. It was stated that Mr. Moss had. -said his re-elec- tion would interfere with his duties as cletk to the School Board, and it was therefore resolved to elect Mr. S. Taylor in his .place. Mr. Handley. and ,Mr. Morris were re-elected:

FIRE AT RIINCORN.—On Wednesday night Mr. W. E. Lea and Mr. W. B. Kay were walking along Halton-road when they observed the bcdroom of a cottage on the other side of the canal to be on tire. The gentlemen crossed the canal in a narrow boat, and quickly awakened the inmates of the cottage, and aided in extinguishing the flames. Had another ten minutes elapsed before the discovery of the fire, the whole cottage would have been in flames. It appeared that a lighted candle had been placed on the dressing table too near the curtains, wipich had become ignited. A chest of drawers was also badly burned. Several children were asleep in the room. A JUBILEE Bow AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Thomas Gibson was charged with assaulting Rachael Tuffe on the 21:4 June. On Jubilee day Daniel Lambert asked the defendant, who was his next door neigh- bour, to go Into his house and have a drink, as the women were going away. He accepted the invitation, and stayed In the house all day. In the evening the women returned, the complainant being with them, and as they were rather noisy, the defendant said to the complainant," Missus, we have been veiy quiet all day, and we don't want any bother now?! She replied "Shut your month." whereupon the de- fendant struck her on the face.—After hearing the evidence the Bench imposetTa fine of 10s, and costs 7s 6d.

Ruticoax BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS AND THE WATER.. WORHS COMP,ANY.—A special meeting 9f the Board of Com- missioners was held at the Town Ball. Waterlon•road, on Thursday, to consider the Liverpool Waterworka Bill, as amended by the House of ,Cominens, and also the petition of the Runcorn, Weiton, and Halton Waterworks Company as to its bearings on the' agreement entered into between the Liverpool Corporation and the Comatiesioners in 1880, and to decide what steps should be taken with rQference to the said bill and petition. Mr. Dobson presided. The sub- jeot was considered in committee, and it was decided to petition in favour of the Liverpool Bill. and for the reten- tion of the clause inserted giving the Board of Commis- sioners, the right to draw, water from the Liverpool water' main at a Esed_charge.

- CRUELTY TO A Lion= AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Captain C. W. Hazlehuret, at Rancorn Police Court, yetterday, William Clarke, hawker, Warrington, was- charged with working a horse whilst it was in Narunfit state, on the 27th June. It appeared that the animal fell down whilst attempting to ascend Bridge-street, near the market, ' and Superintendent Hollingsworth instructed P.C. Smith to ascertain the cause. The constable found the horse was as stiff in its hind quarters that.. it could.not get up until-rho cart was taken away. The horse was taken to the stables of Mr. Yarwood, who deposed tbat the bind fetlockloints were ossified. The animal was also in poor condition, and utterly unfit for work of way kind. Inspector Aplin. R.S.P.C.A., said the horse was only fit to be destroyed. The prisoner would not, consent to the destruction of the horse, and he was fined £2 and costs, £1 Oa 61. In default he went to goal for a mouth. TES ALLEGED ,THEFT OF A HOME AND CART.— On Friday, at the Town Hall, James Oeogagban' Thomas Ed- ward Jackson, and Hugh Hughes, all of Widnes, were broturbt up on remand charged with stealing a horse and cart, and a quanthy of groceries, the property of Margaret Hampton,a carrier residing at Parr.—The evidence was to the effect that on the night of the Newton Maces, Mrs. Hanpaton called at the Tipping Arms Ina, Bold. While she Was in the hones she was told that the prisoners had driven away with the eat. Therwere followed, overtaken, and subsequently apprebended:4-Lieutenant,Colonel Pilkiugton , said be was glad the prisoners had been in custody. He cansikiered it a foolish drunken spree.—Mr.Riley represented ,the prisoner Hughes, and said his client hal only accepted the invitation of the other prisoners to get behind the cart and have .11 ride towards Widnes. He had testimonials tiom his master, under whom he had worked twelve years, and others as to character.—Lieut -Colonel Pilkington recona- naendedllughes to be more ctreful as to bis company in the future, sod discharged the prisoners.

THE RUNCORN JUBILEE CELEBRATIONS —A meeting of the Runcorn Jtibilee Committee was held on Thursday even• ing. at the Town Hall. Mr. P. Speakman presided, and there was a good attendance. Mr. Holland, rnana4.r a`, Ibe hank, WM appointed treasurer in the place of the late Mr. Chorltna, and a vote of condolence was pa=sed to Mrs. Charlton and family.—A cordial vote of thanks was ac- corded to Superintendent Hollingwenth for the admirable manner in which he performed his duties on Jubilee day. Votes of thanes were also passed to Mr. Kirkham for the use of the field, to the secretaries for their valua- ble services, to Mr. George Bellany, who gave the tickets for the children, and to the vatioui sub•committers. The Vicar also moved a vote'' of thanks to the chairman, Mr. Speakman. The Rev.l George Wood e•conded the proposition, which was coaled. Mr. Jauion announced that he had collected 30e. on the river steamers towards the celebration Toe accounts showed that there had been expsnded for the aged poor £2O Be 2d ; echool children, £1131; fireworks, £l6. The total expenditure amounted to £196. Out of the surplus it wee cdcided to give each of the four and who voluntarily took part in the procession a donation of 10s. It may be elated that £lO was contributed by Mr. R. Verdin. M.P., Mr. J. T. Brunner, and Meagre. Wigg Bros. and Steele. THROWING A KNIFE AT RUNOORN.—At Runcorn Petty' Sessions, on Mood.", before Captain C. W. Hazlehnrst, Jno. Morrie, manager 'of a shop in Bridge-street. belonging to Mr. Johnson, wholegale grocer, St. Helens, was brought up on' remand charged with having unltto ally arid maliciounlY wounded Thomas Kennedy, a carter, also employed by Mr. Johnsen.—Mr. Madden, of Liverpool. appeared for the,* feedant. and asked that the charge should he reduced to one of common assault. Kennedy said be had no wish to press the case, but Superintendent Hollingworth objected to the application, and the magistrates declined to accede to Mr. Madden's requeat —.The prosecutor stated that on Wednesday morning, the 22ad June, he was in the shop, and as be teamed the prisenee, the latter said he would stop him from coming that way, and threw a piec3 of bacon at him. The 'prosecutor threw the bacon beck at the prisoner, who then picked up a large carving knife, and aimed it at the pro. sectitor. The weapon struck him on the left side, and then felt to the ground. At this time there Was Only a space of four or five feet between them. Both men attempted to strike each ether with their fists until Constable Millington arrived. The prisener had sent for the constable, who took the men to the police office. Subsequently Dr. McDougall examined the injured man and advieed him to stay in bed three or four days, and be did so. The blood•smeared clothes the'proseentor was wearing at the time were pro- duced, and the cuts made by the knife were shown. In cross-examination the prosecutor said he had his beck to the prisoner and he did not see the prisoner throw the knife. He bad a perfect right to pass through the shop in the way he was doing at the time.—James Costello. asele- tent at the shop, deposed that the prisoner told Kennedy that he must. find another way out. of the shop, and Ken- nedv turned backend asked " Have you any more weights to throw." This referred to a " row." that !sad occurred en the Monday night when the prisoner threw a weight at Kennedy. Witness corroborated the prosecutor's evidence. —By Mr. Madden The prisoner threw the weight at Kennedy because he went in the bakehouse. Kennedy had ho right to be tbere.—Dr. McDougall stated that he ex• entitled the prosecutor and found a clean cut wound under the left arm. The wound was a little overen inch in length, and penetrated an inch and a half under the skin in the direction of the shoulder blade. The wound WAR in a dan- gerous part, and it wee such a one that might have been in- flicted by the knife produced —By Mr. Madden : Kennedy must have had his arm uplifted for the knife to have struck him in the position it did. A similar wound might have been produced by the prosecutor rushing against the knife In the prisoner's band, hut it was more probable that the knife was thrown.--P.C. Millington deposed to apprehend- ing the prisoner, who. when charged, said "I did it, bat did not intend to hurt laim.”—The prieoner. who reserved his defence, MS committed to the sessions for trial. The pri- saner surrendered to his bail at Knutsford Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday. and pleaded guilty —The Chairman (Mr. Horatio Lloyd) said the prisoner was now, no doubt, ex- ceedingly sorry that be gave way to temper and injured the prosecutor, who had just shown a very good •feelint towards him by saying what he geoid do on his behalf. The magistrates were anxious to punish him without in- flicting unnecessary degradation. and they had therefore decided to fine him a and as a matter of forin he would be imprisoned till the fine was paid.— ' The money was immediately paid, and the prisoner was liberated. '—" Truth"' says It is somewhat curious that Lord Ilartington and Mr. Chamberlain, although they profess to be the closest allies, never meet on the same platform. When one speaks, there isalWays a letter read from the other, declaring his regret thaeowing to circumstances he cannot appear. • REDUCTION OF Films TO TILE ISLEOF MAR.—The directors of the Manx Lioe, being desirous of mak- ing their boats even More popular, if that is possible, 'than 'before, have decided to..issue cheap .return ,tickais to the Isle of Man, available for 28 days. at 8s and 4s, first and second saloon respectively; and there can be no,doubt that-this-will tend to make these boats still more attractive to the 'visitors 'to that island.

THE DROUGHT IN CHUSHIRIL—The exceptional and protracted drought is causing serious incenve- nience to the residents on the Bickerton range of hills, in Cheshire. In the best of times the inhabi- tants have largely to depend pa the pits and rain- water supplies generally. The pits have now been dry for over a week,. an the water is being fetched many miles in carts And hawked about the district. Such a drought has not been experienced for some years. CADISHEAD.—The Rev David Clegg, congregk- tionalist minister, of Cidishead, conducted an open- air service in Heays-street, in the above-named village on Tuesday evening. Mr. Sankey's hymns were used and sung by the choir and a „large con- gregation which assembled. The rev. gentleman dis- coursed on the words of Christ, _" Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in My name, He will give it you," to an attentive audience, many of whom were mothers with their children. PUBLIC SYMPATHY WITH THE CliAnamiarEns.— Speaking at a meeting at Bolton on Wednesday night, in aid of the starving chainmakers on strike at Cradley Heath, Mr. R. Juggins, a deputation from ! Staffordshire, graphically described the mode of living and rate of wages paid to this afflicted por- tion of the English race, who were haying their very life's blood drawn from them by the disgrace- ful, unchristianlike attitude of• the masters. Sup- port, though long awaited, besadded, is now com- ing. A co-operative society has been formed in ! Manchester to carry on chain works in Staffordshire and rescue the strikers. • LANCASHIRE ANNUAL SESSIONS.—At the annuEd General Session for the county of Lancaster, which was held at Preston, on Thursday, Mr. J. T. Hib- bert presiding, the difficulty which has arisen be- tween the county authorities and various boroughs Which have hitherto bad the services of the county police was again referred to. 'lt was intimsied that the county justices were willing to do all they could to meet the convenience of those boroughs,•but they. could net act illegally. Resolutions were afterwards adopted approving of agreements with the Corpora- tions of Over Darwen, Middleton, Heywood, and Chorley•whereby the consolidation of the county ' and borou.gh police establishments is brought about. MANCHESTER EXHIBITION. In thP Queen's Bench, on Wednesday, the Attorney-General moved, on behalf of the Justices and Chief Constable of the county of Lancaster, for an injunction against the Watch Committee and Chief Constable of Man- chester, restraining them froin exercising constabu- lary duties at the Jubilee Exhibition, which is out- side the boundaries •of the city. Their Lordships refused the injunction, as it did not Eimer that the city police were doing anything which a private individual might not do, and the balance of conve- nience being in favour of the course adopted.—The attendance at the Manchester Jubilee Exhibition on Wednesday was 19,099, making a total since the opening of 1475.393. Lrvan.PooL ExammoN.—The Jubilee celebra- tions at the •Liverpooi Exhibition which have been I under the patronage of the Queen, and which have , been on a more extensive scale than anything seen out of London, have been a great success, and have attracted over one hundred thousand people. The display of the trophies of peace and war, which • takes place in the palace, has been a fitting oom-. megnoration of Her Majesty's reign. The special attractions at Liverpool Exhibition during the ! forthcoming week will include a grand Scottish ! athletic festival, in which some of the champions !of the North will take part. The band of the Royal Scots is engaged, as well as the famous Cameroman pipers. This fete is •under the patronage of the I Caledonian Association.

THE ACCIDENTS TO ISIA3 OF /4 KS' BOATS. —ln a paragraph which has appeared in some papers it is stated that the" Lancashire Witch" met with an accident, and that her passengers did not land until Sunday. As a matter of fact, she did not leave Ramsey until between 10 and 11 p.m. on Saturday. The accident was of the simplest character—viz., the breaking away of one of the blades of her propeller. She proceeded under her own steam (not in tow) to her anchorage. The managers have arran_ed to put her in dry dock and to replace her broken propeller with a new one, which will, it is expected, be of greater strength, and give the "Lancashire Witch" a considerably quicker speed. Regarding the mishap to the Victoria, a correspondent says :—"A slight accident didoccur, which might occur to any boat, but there was not the slightest confusion on board. There is no truth in the statement that the passengeni were tran- shipped to the Prince of Wales, and there is no truth in the statement that the Queen Victoria had to be towed into Douglas. The repairs were quietly done by the staff on board temporarily, and she ' went a full speed into Douglas without the least , help from any boat or anyone." LAWN Tionnts.— wareingten v. „ • THE J UB MBE' aRLEBRATION' AT CROFT. The Jubilee was celebrated by the parishioners of CrOft on Saturday in a loyal and enthusiastic manner. At half-past one o'clock the children of the parish. from three to 15 years of age, to the number of about 260. assembled at the Board School, when the Rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, gave an address on her Majesty's long and happy reign, and afterwards read the special prayers appointed. Afterwards those who had not previously receiVed medals were presented with them. Shortly after two o'clock a ' procession was formed. At five o'clock 40 of the aged people in the parish, 60 years of age and over, sat down to a substantial tea. The young people , and friends also partook of tea at the same tune,l and afterwards the committee, teachers, band, waiters and waitresses, the total number provided , with tea in the field and schoolroom being about 450. After tea all assembled in the field, where sports took place. They created much interest and amusement, as some of the events were very keenly contested. The band afterwards played a selection of music for (lancing, &c.. in a creditable manner, under the conductorship of Mr. F. W. Ball, until dusk, when hearty'cheers were given for the Rector, churchwardens, the ladies' committees, namely, Mrs Reginald Owen, een. (president), Mrs Kirkman, Miss Southern, Mrs Isaac Moines, Mrs Beckett, Mrs Joe. Whiston, Mrs Peter Waywell, Mrs David Wnywell, • Mrs Joseph Green. Mrs Isaac Green, and Mrs James Green—Mr. F. W. Rail, the hon, secretary, the sub- scribers, and the band. Balloons were sent up, and at dusk the band marched to the school, where the National Anthem and "Rule Brittania ” were played, , after which some of the aged people and others ad- journed to the large pavilion at the General Elliott Hotel, where dancing was heartily engaged in until eleven o'clock, to the strains of Mr. Stirrup's quad- rille band, of Warrington.

A DRSEETER AT WIDNES. - At Widnes Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. H. W. Deacon, William Brothers :belonging to the South Lancashire Regi m ent stationed at Warrington, was charged with being an absentee on the 21st May last. The prisoner since this date has served a month's imlirisontnent for assaulting P.S. Stricklann, and hn was now sent to Walton to await an escort.

THE CORNBROOK EMPLOGION.--On Friday morn- ing, Colonel Majendie, Inspector of Explosivea; Home Office, and Mr. Du Pre, Government chemist, arrived in Manchester, and proceeded to the works of Messrs Roberts, Dale, and Company, at Corn- brook, where the disastrous explosion occurred on the 23rd ult. The investigations into the causes which led to the explosion were continued, and in all probability a report will be presented at the adjourned inquest. • ACCIDENT TO SIR W. C. BROOKS, M.P.—We regrei to learn that Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, Bart., M.P., while walking to the House of Commons, on Thdrs- day, slipped on some polished pavement and fraa- tured the wrist of his left arm. He drove immedi- ately to Mr. Marshall, F.RS., had the bone set, and then went to the House. He was too late for the first set of divisions, but attended the evening de- bates, and, remained in the House until half-past one on Friday morning. A WARRINGTON MAN IN TROUBLE AT Sr. HELENS. L.-At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Thursday, Thos. Swift, of Warrington' was charged with assaulting P.C. Pope. Sergeant Wolsey stated that about hall= past eleven on Wednesday night he heard screams proceeding from Cropper's-hill, and on going to the place ayoung woman named Margaret Basnett said that prisoner and another Dian had assaulted her. Prisoner struck her again in the constable's. pre- sence, and, as he refused to give his name and ad- dress, he was taken into custody. P.C. Pope came to witness's assistance, upon which he tripped Polie and fell on him. Witness pulled prisoner up, and during a severe struggle he struck Pope several times in the face. cutting his lip, making his nose Weed, and taking the Skin from his left arm. He was handcuffed and taken to the Town Hall. A fine of .£1 and costs was imposed, or 28 days' imprison- ment.

THE LODGER QUESTION AT EARLESTOWN.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs It Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W. Fe Gooch, Mr. H. J. Longton mentioned the case in which Mr. W. Urquhart, tailor and draper, Earlestown, was sum- moned for illegally distraining upon the goods of. a Mrs Georgina Williams, who had lodged In Oxford- street. Mr. Longton stated that an order was made

for the return of-the goods, arid also for thepay- ment of .42 17s, costs incurred in the proceedings. That order had not been complied with, and he (Mr. Longton) had to apply for a distresi warrant against Mr. Urquhart so as to enforce the order. The Clerk (Mr. Nicholson)': You will have to prove the sert. ' vice of the order upoh Mr. Urquhart. Mr. Longten Police-sergeant Commins served the order, and he is . unwell and unable to attend here this morning. I did not'know this nntil I came a few minutes ago. • P.C. Spencer stated that P.S. COmmins was ill in bed, and could not attend, and the Bench asked Mr. Longton to renew his application at the nnt court:. Mr. Longton consented to do so. •

TUE JIIBLLER AT DARESBITRY.-011 Thursday last week about 120 people. partook of a most ex- cellent tea in the schoolroom, in commemoration of- Her Majesty's Jubilee. The school was most taste- fully and profusely deborated by Messrs Johnson, of Warrington, at the expense of Mrs W. C. Jones, of the Oaklanda, and bunting of every description was to be seen both inside and ' outside. Provfsions in. abundance were given by Mrs .Tones, of the TErns, and a ham by Mr. P. Darbyshire. Near the centre of one of the tables stood a large and magnificent cake, standing 2 feet high, manufactured by Bollands, the celebrated confectioners of Chester, and presented by the kind lady of the Elms. After ample justice had been done to the good things set before the guests, the cake was cut and handed round,' to the great enjoyment of all. As a more lasting memorial of the occasion, Mr. and Mrs Jones, of the Oaklands, presented a beautiful brooch to every female, and. to every male a pretty. searf-pin. After tea, many availed themselves Of the opportunity of seeing the beautiful gardens at the Oaklands, and at 8-30 a mu- sical entertainment was given, for which Missi Whitley most ably accompanied. The singing of the National Anthem, and cheers for the generosity and willing hands of all who assisted in the conduct of the proceedings, brought to close a happy day. On Friday afternoon the school children of Dares- bury and district, numbering about 400. assembled for the " Jubilee " service in church, and afterwards, marched in procession, headed by a band, to Newton Bank Park, which was kindly thrown open by Mr. Rodger. The Rev. Canon Heron and Messrs Percival and Hewitt, members of the School Board, drove behind the procession. Arriving at Newton Bank, the children were directed underneath the shade of the trees, where they partook of a good tea prol vided for them, and spent the remainder of the day in games, &c. THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY.—In another column there will be found the prospectus of the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company. Applications for ordinary shares are invited; £42 only will be required to , be paid on allotment, the remainder being paid by- instalments at intervals of not less than three months each, and not exceeding .£1 each, or £2 lOs in any 12 months. These easy terms are particularly advantageous to small capitalists, who have faith in the undertaking, and wish to !invest what they can save 'during the period of the making of , the canal. Four per cent, interest is to be paid out of capital for the four years whilst the canal is un-. der construction. There is a fair prospect of • a , higher rate of interest being obtained afterwards, judging from the profitable character of other canals. Preference shares will be issued to bear 5 ! per cent. interest, but of course no more thaii 5 per I cent, will be paid, however profitable the uadertak- ' ing may become. It is satisfactory to oW • serve that the Company are grad tfally over- : coming all their difficulties. Yesterday afternoon_ jat three o'clock, the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany's Preference Share Bill, came before the Standing Orders Committee in the House of Lords, the Duke of Buckingham presiding. Non-compli-- ance with the tanding Orders was reported by the, j Examiner, in consequence of the time when the bill was deposited. namely, the Bth June, the Stand— • ing Orders providing that bills shall be deposited in ' December of the year preceding that in which they ' are introduced. No opposition was offered to the • bill. Mr. Coats, who appeared for the promoters, I stated that applications for fresh shares had been, made to the amount of £176,000 since he prepared • ; his statement for the company, and the whole of the capital would be forthcoming when this bill' passed. The committee passed the bill, and it will be read a second time next week. It is pretty safe' now to predict that the bill will become law. BOWLING.—J. SHAW AND W. GLHAVE POO £4O.

—At Bank Quay Subscription Bowling .Green. War- rington, on Saturday afternoon, an exrotinz contest was witnessed between the above men, who had. agreed to play a game of bowls, 101 up, for £2O aside. As the men reside in different parts of the, town, the interest in the event was great, and the large company that assembled around the green, which was in excellent order, included most of the _

_ sporting fraternity of the neighbourhood. At the commencement of play Shaw's partisans felt confi- dent of strcess, but he was 'fortunate to win as Gleave, at the. latter portion of the game, was 2o in front, the scores standing--Gleave, 83; Shaw. 63.. Shaw made the first 4 points; then Gleave made a. I run of 7, and afterwards went to 15, to. Shaws' 9. Shaw now got the jack, and, playing well on a short mark, he scored 25 leave's 20. Up to half game, both men alternately made short runs, Gleave scoring a 9. 7, two s's, and a 4; whilst Shaw put together two 4's and a 6: the scores being—Gleave, 52; Shaw, 45. After a short interval Gleave made .a rim of 10, to which, Shaw responded with a 7 and 6; the game being called— Shaw 59, Gleave 65. The latter afterwards reached 76 to 60, 79 to 62, and 83 to 6.'3. The game • now looked a foregone conclusion for Gleave, but 'Shaw began to play much better, making 22 to his oppo- nent's 4, and eventually the game was called." 92 all," "94 all." and "96 all." The excitement ;was now great, and each man was well cheered as he played his bowl in close proximity to the "jack." The result •of the game proved Shaw to be victorious by two points. At the last end Gleave led the "jack," and played a good bowl, but Shaw beat it; then Gleave with his second bowl knocked Shaw's wood off the green, but the latter player was again successful with his second bowl. The score at the finish of the game was—Shaw 101, Gloave 99, Mr.. Henry Gittins, of the Swan Inn. was stakE. and referee.

div.head: " TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: " TOUCH AND GO."
The dry weather is interft ring with business. Everywhere there is a cn —not for " more light," but " more water.'' Even the milk- men are complaining,

- On. Saturday, the old folk of Earlestown Were treated to a Jubilee dinner, which was served in good st),le. And they were Old Folks; there were 123 of them, and the average of their ages was 71 yeats.

The Queen has given something to corn- memorate her Jubilee ; she has bestowed her thanks. It is as well to be courteous ; civility costs nothing. And then we have it on good authority that we should be grate- ful to the great that.they do us no harm.

Mr. Chamberlain once said, "I hat,?. coer- cion ; I hate the name; I hate the thing." On Monday evening he voted with the Toiies for making coercion perpetual; and yet there are people who swear by Mr. Chamberlain's consistency.

Students of the career and character of the member for West Birmingham—and there are many at the present moment—should turn to the first article in the "Westminster Review" for June. It is written in a mas- terly style by a writer who knows his subject from top to bottom. He is just to Mr. Cham- berlain, but that means that he is hard on him, for he pelts him with quotations from his own speeches.

Messrs. Whiteman and Cos, milk contrac- tors, have slipped through the hands of an Inspector who wished to have their milk analysed by pleading that the Act does not apply to wholesale dealers. The magistrates upheld this view of the law, which implies that little fish masr be caught in the net, and that the big ones can break through it.

At the opening of the June Quarter Ses- sions. at Chester, on Monday, I-us Hon-mr Judge Horatio Lloyd, in charging the Grand Jury reported another very satisfactory dim intition in crime in the country." This would be a good reason, wouldn't it? for,treatina the county to a Jubilee Coercion Bill? That is what they do for Ireland under similar circumstances.

At Daresbury Sessions, on Tuesday, Mr. T 0• Speakman, of the Saracen's Head, Wil !durspool, was fined for keeping his house open after hours on Jubilee day. Mr. E. Greenall, who was in the chair, advised him not to do such a thing again. Very good advice, and we dare say Mr. Speakman will comply. Indeed, we may venture to pro- phecy that he will not offend at the next Jubilee of the Sovereign's reign.

Mr. Boardman, farmer, of Rainford, ought to be supported in the stand he is making on behalf of a public footpath near Rainford. The suminous taken 3ut against him by the Railway Company was dismissed on Monday on the ground that the St. Helens Police Court had no jutisdiction. It is just possible that the Company may take further proceedings, and in that case Mr. Boardman. who is fightrng a public battle, should be supported by the public. On Wednesday, at St. Helens, the police- man's lot was for once a happy one. The police division is being broken up in con- sequence of the formation of a borough police force; and pres •ntations were made to Superintendent Johnston and Inspector Whit- taker (through Mrs. WhiLtaker). From the speeches made, it is evident that the leave- taking touched their hearts. Officers and men have had a genuine regard for each other, so much so that it seems almost a pity to break into such a happy family.

It seems that the Captain of the Shannon has put his foot in it in hauling down and taking possession of the green flag which was floating over an Irish yacht the other day. Lord George Hamilton explained, in the House of Commons, on Tuesday, that the Captain was " technically in error and must restore the flag." Umph ! It was recently stated, on behalf of the Government, that the Coercion Bill did not create a new offence— except " technically." When it is passed Irish M.P.'s will be put in gaol " technically ;" and when things have got to the worst " technically," the present Government will be snuffed out "technically." So be it.

A contemporary gives the following as "the champion jubilee story " ; " P.C. Wressel, of West Carnforth, has a hen. which on Jubilee Day laid an egg, one side of which was flat, whilst on the -Other side there was a raised substance bearing in shape a close resemblance to a crown." But this is small beer. An old lady of our acquaintance, who is exactly the same age as the Queen, found, when she awoke on Jubilee Day, a crown on her head ; and something in her pocket which the learned in such matters say

H. iWartarmt & Co., 47, Farringdon•street, London, E C, the proprietors of Warner's SAFE Care :—" I feel that it is my duty to tell you of, and thank you for, the great benefit I Oave derived Irqm the use of your wonderful medicine. For many years past I have been a great sufferer from what the - doctors call 'lung trouble,' and my life has been really most miserable; the pain in my back, and especially in that -Portion just underneath' the shoulder blades, has been mos Intense; fray nerves have been so unstrung that I found it impossible to sleep at night. and, being deprived of my • Much-needed rest, my general strength bectme such as really to Prevent my attending properly to the simplest household duties ;I was always down-hearted, and sometimes tbouglit I would:consider it a mercy if it were God's will that I shen!ri be summoned hence; but I decided at last, the doenrs failing, to try Warner's SAFE Care, and have been a diffsrent woman since I began its use. It is now three weeks ti nee I got the first bottle of the Warner's SAFE Caro, end all my faenily are rejoiced at the change for the better ; my pains have nearly all left me, my nights are now more re.tfal, and my cough, which I forgot to mention, and my difficulty of breathing, are things of the past. I now fcel as though I had something to live for, and am con- fident that I owe all to the wonderful virtues of your medicine." Mr.. W. Asked now if he had found his missing limbs he replied that they were all there, and that he felt better. lie was remanded to the Workhouse. TUESDAY—Before Alderman Sutton.

ST2AYING HORSES—Joseph Weetwood, a travelling hawker, was summoned for allowing two horses to stray on the highway at Antrobus on the 26th May. A letter was I read stating that the defendant was unable to appear as he bad been summoned to attend before another court.—He was fined 2e 61 and costs. A WILDEIISPOOL PUBLICAN FINED.—Mr. T. 0. Speak- man, landlord of the Saracen's Head public house, Wilder. spool, was summoned for having kept his premises open for the sale of intoxicating liquors during a time that they ought to have been closed. The following persons who be- longed to Warrington, were also summoned for having been on the premises. viz.—Fred Taylor, Thomas Stokes, Thos. Crossley, Henry A. Powell, Teomas Attwell, Edward Bul- lock, George It. Williams, Charles Davies, William L. Fair- hurst, James Senkey, and Thomas Waghorn. It appeared that the offence was committed about eleven o'clock on Tuesday night, the 21st inst. Two police officers seeing the door of defendant's house open went and found the men named at the bar, and one of them was receiving a glass of beer fr. to Mrs. Speakman, to whom be gave 6d, and re- ceived hack the change —Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, Warring- ton, who appeared for all the defendants, pleaded guilty on their b their. In extenuation he mentioned that between ten a d eleven o'clock a waggonette drove up to the Sara- cen's Head, and the occupants who were travellers were supplied with refreshments. The defendants were at the time returning from the bonfire which had been lighted at Hill Warren the same night, and seeing the door open they went into the house, and Mrs. Speakman not knowing them, then.tht they were also travellers and supplied them. The beach decided to fine Speakman el and costs, and the other -defendants were dismissed on payment of costs. The bench Intimated that they were of opinion that Speakman shoul I Day the coats of the other defendants, and Mr, Jenkins said he would see that that was done. _ _ .

THROWING STONRS.—A dharce of throwing stones in Deacon-road en the 19th June was brought against a youth named Rimmer, who was remanded for a month in order that the police might observe how he conducted himself daring that period.

THREATS. Joseph Ford, seer., was charged with threatening to assault Sarah Fleet, widow, on the 26th June. Mr. Knowles was for the defendant. It was alleged that the defendant met the woman in the street. and raising his clenched hand, threatened her violence if she pawned any more goods for his wife. Later in the clay, he ran after her with a knife and threatened to take her life. The defendant denied having a knife in his !.and, and stated that he only said he would "lick" her. He was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months.

Weisaiworrow V. Itosnomag.—This match was played at Warrington, on Saturday, and resulted in a draw favourable to the home team. Having won the toss, Warrington com- menced with J. J. Crosfield and Armstrong. Runs came fast, especially from Dain, and 54 was telegraphed for one wicket. The bowlers got the ball to bump, and from a bumping ball Armstrong was caught at mid-off. Denton came in and played carefully, but was taken at wicket by Wadsworth standing back. Clarke, the next corner, began well by driving Holmes to the off for four, and in the next over-driving B. urn hard back for another quartette. Warren went on for Holmes, and Dain for Bruce, but runs came quickly. Crosfield played very steadily, yet could net get the bowling away. Three half volleys on the one side were punished by Clarke for fours, and at 148 he was taken from a fast rising ball at slip. Crosfield was caught nine runs later for a well-played 73. Until he reached 50 his innings was very good, but at this score he became a little unsteady. At 63 he returned an easy catch to Bruce, hat that player dropped it. Carpenter and Podoore put on 20 for the last wicket, the innings closing for 198. Bruce got three wickets for 41, white Warren got 5 for 75. Rusholme com- menced disastrously; four men were out for 12, and the fifth fell at 25. Plitt now joined E. Wadsworth, and the score ran on to 76, chiefly by tbe hitting of the last-named. Wadsworth fell at 89, and the next two deserve the credit of saving their aide from defeat. Clarke and Smith played the bowling carefully. but did not attempt to score much, contenting themselves by keeping up their ends. Change after change was tried, but to no purpose, until a minute before time, when Smith was bowled by a leg break from from Podrnore. Holmes played the remaining three balis, and the game was left drawn at eight wickets for 117. Had either of two chances keen taken when Smith and Clarko were together, the home team inight have won the match. Tinsley howled well almost throughout, getting five wickets for 36 runs. Score :

SAD SUICIDE NEAR WARRINGTON.

A sad suicide occurred on Sunday. It appears that a widow, named Caroline Beckett, 25 years .of age, who had lived in Mill-lane,Warrington, on that day sent her two children to a friend's house at Winwick, and then, so far as can be ascertained, threw herself into the canal near Walton Arches. On Monday afternoon, Mr. H. B. White, the deputy coroner, held an inquiry regarding her death at the Stag's Head Inn, Walton, when evidence to the fol- lowing effect was taken. Mary Dean said that the body alge had seen was that of her late daughter, Caroline Beckett,who was 25 years of age. Witness had never noticed anything Iparticular about her since her husband's death, ex.- ; cept that she complained frequently of pain in the I head. On Sunday deceased sent her two children to witness.—A Juryman: You had no suspicion when ' she sent you the children? No.—You thought there was nothing unusual? You had no suspicion of anything happening wrong? No.—ln answer to further questions, witness said she did not know what the cawse of her daughter's action might be. Witness could not tell how deceased was in circum- stances. _ _

William Connor, forge labourer, 2, Grimes's-yard, off Bank-street, Warrlngton, said that on Sunday he was on the bank of the Old Quay Canal at Wal— ton Inferior, between two and three o'clock in the afternoon. He was sitting down, and seemed to be. going to Oeep when he heard someone shouting that there was a person in the canal. He then saw part of a woman's hair and dress in the water. He took off his clothes, entered the water, and, having seized hold of the woman's dress, he swam to the side with the body. Then he lifted her on to the bank and went for a policeman. The body was full dressed, but the woman's bonnet was over her face. In answer to the jury, witness said he did not see any bathers about at the time in question.

Edward Dean, brother of the deceased, said that the letter produced, which had been. found on the table in the kitchen of the deceased's house, was in his sister's handwriting. The letter read as fob.. ,lows :—" Dear ----. Don't frown upon my chil- dren. Give all there is for them. I have never been happy since I left my little home in Lloyd- street.. IT my dear George was here. Tell James that as he has not sent that, it will do for another purpose. Do not part with any of my clothes, or George's. Leave them for dear my children. I have never been happy since he died, or knew that he was going to." Witness added that the words "Tell James," Ste., referred to some money. William Jenks, landlord of the Green Man beer- house, off Lovely-lane, said that he knew deceased, and her late husband. He Mid seen deceased frequently since the death of her late husband. Deceased had lived just off Lovely-lane, at the back of the White House, She lad two cottages and a shop, which her late husband bought shortly before his death. He left them to her. The cottages would each bring her in about 3s 6d a week, an She lived at the shop. She was in witness's house on Friday night, from about 9-3 D to 10 o'clock. She had a glass of beer every night for supper.—The Coroner: Since her husband's death has she said anything that would lead you to suppose she was very unhappy? No; she has been keeping company with some young man. Her husband and me were great friends, and I told her about going with this young man. There did not seem to be anything unusual the matter with her on Friday night.—tiave you any idea where she has been since? Not the slightest.—A Juryman: What sort of a character had the person she kept company with? He has been labouring at Monks' a short time, but I have keard since yester- day that he got discharged from there. I have heard that he is not working anywhere now, but I have no proof of that.—How long has she kept company with him? I hear from about a month after her husband died.—A Juryman: She must not have thought much of her "dear George" then.—Witness further deposed that the deceased was not a person who took much drink; she never took above one glass of beer to her supper.—A Juryman: Do you think it troubled her mind when she got entangled with this young man, and when she thought of the children afterwards? I cannot ' read ber mind.—Was it correct that they were to

be married to-day ? Not that I am aware of.—A Juror: That is what has been reported. P.C. John Bennett (319C.C.C.), •stationed at Lower Walton; said that be received laformation at about four o'clock on Sunday afternoon of a body having been found in the canal. He went there and found the body of the deceased, who was dressed, very neatly, in black, 'Witness searched the pockets and found a silver watch and guard, aphotograph of the deceased, her husband, and their two chil- dren, and a funeral card of her late husband. In her skirt pocket was half a sovereign and other money, and she had on her linger three rings—wed- ding, keeper, and mourning rings. The funeral card i referred to stated that it was n "affectionate re- membrance of George Beckett, who departed this life February 2nd, 1887, aged 32 years." There was. also on it the following verse— / "Day by day hie wife does miss him, Words would fail her loss to tell ; But in heaven she hopes to meet him, Evermoremith him to dwell." Witness Jenks, recalled, said that the deceased and her children lived alone. The Coroner informed the jury that that was all the evidence to be brought before them. They had a letter that was identified as having been written by the deceased, and, coupled with the fact of the body being afterwards found in thee water, they I could have little doubt about the intention of the deceased at the time she wrote it. Possibly she hadi read an account of an inquest held at that sem I house the other day, which might lead her to,choose the place she had done. They had also heard that I she sometimes suffered from pains in the head, and'l he thought that they could fairly attribute the un- fortunate occurrence to temporary insanity. In answer to the jury, witness Bennett said that be understood that the name of the man with-whom deceased had been keeping company was lienwright. —A Juryman: I think we should have him here. Is he a decent labouring man ?—Mr. Jenks: I know himt well enough as a customer, but he just comes- for an odd glass. I have not seen much of him for this last twelve months; I have nothing to say against the man, because I have nothing wrong against him. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide by drowning herself in the Old Quay Canal, she being at the time tem- porarily insane. •

div.head: NOTES BY THE. WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE. WAY.

- The international tournament which was held on the Alexandra Park grounds, on Thursday. Friday, and Satan. day of last week, was an interesting event in the cycling world. It brought together same representative wheelmen of no fewer than nine nationalities. So far as racing was concerned the tournament was a success, but it is said that the pe.cuniary results do not encourage a repetition. Some fine racing was witnessed in the one mile tricycle handicap, the winner being E. Kiderlen, a Dutch representative, who did the distance in 2 ruin. 59 3-5 secs. This rider also won the 2 miles international scratch tricycle race in 6 min. 41 secs, The half-mile bicycle handicap and the 5 miles bicycle scratch race were won by W. A. Illston, of the Speedwell 8.C., the former in 1 min. 18 3 5 secs, and the latter in 15 ruin. 4 2-5 secs. F. J. Lees, of Leicester, secured first prize in the five-miles professional scratch race his time being 15 min. 4 2-5 secs. The St. Helens Club secured another easy victory on Saturday. when Dingle had to put up with a defeat of 148 tuns to 82. The home team (especially Jeffreys, A. Simm, Massey, Chandley, and Hinciley) batted well, and gave the visitors plenty of leather chasing. On the Dingle men go- ing to the wicket they were unable to withstand the St. Helens pro. (Butler) who took nine wickets for 15 runs. H. Maxwell alone got into double figures (15), but the extras amounted to a total of 21.

The Southport eleven came to play St: Helens Recrea- tion on Saturday, but the latter occupied the wickets during the whole of the afternoon, and when stumps were drawn there were three wickets to fall. The score was 182 for seven wickets.
- Pilkington's Plate Works met Runcorn on the ground of the latter, and the home team was defeated by 71 runs to 52.

The match between Lancashire and Clazshire, at Stock- port, was concluded on Saturday, the former gaining an easy victory by an innings and four runs. Lancashire had made 199 in the first innings, and Cheshire in their first essay having only put on 66, followed on. At the drawing of the stumps on Friday eight the Cestrians had made 40. for the loss of one wicket. Mr. Crostield, the Cheshire cap- tain, played splendid cricket for his 52. At lunch the score stood at eight wickets for 128. Afterwards th. destructive Lancashire bowling disposed of the two remaining men in three minutes. On the same day Gloucestershire suffered a crushing defeat by Surrey by an innings and 104 runs to spare; the Liverpool District eleven gained a victory over Yorkshire by 38 runs ; Oxford University beat Middlesex in a single innings with 229 runs to spare; Nottinghamshire beat Marylebone club and ground by 28 runs; and the Essex cricketers were victorious over Hampsnira by , 25. runs.

Warrington met Rusholme on Saturday on the home ground, and ran up a total of 198 rms ; to this Crosfield contributed no less than 73, while Clarke had 48 to his credit, and Carpenter with 29,and Armstrong with 20, came next. Rust:mime, for the loss of eight wickets, made 117,50 that the match was pretty well contested. Surrey, for the first time this seasen, have this week sue- tamed defeat, Oxford University being the victots, by 82' runs, of a very hard-fought game. This result was mainly due to the successful bowling of Mr. Backland, who took five wickets with astonishing rapidity for 11 runs. Briggs gave a good account of himself in the match be- tween Lancashire and Kent at Gravesend On the first day, Monday, he bit brilliantly for 65. He was in for an hour and a half, and made six fours and eight threes. Oa Tues- day, when the game was concluded in favour of Lancashire by an innings and 62 runs in hand, Briggs was successful with the ball. In the first innings of Kent he ,obtained seven wickets for 44 runs.

The Northern Counties Lawn Tennis Championship Meeting was concluded at o.d Trafford on Saturday. Miss L. llod now holds the Northern Championship, having beaten Miss Watson, and Mr. H. Grove has again won the Association Silver Challenge Cup.

SILVER ON THE BRAlN.—Senater Fair, one of the richest men in the Sena.° of the United States, being worth over one hundred millions of dollars, is a man of marked peru— Rarities. He it largely interested in silver mining, and in more senses than one may be said to have "silver on the brain," for about the commencement of his successful career, he received a blow which frac ured his skull, and was only saved from death by the operation of trepanning—that is to say. a plate of silver was inserted in the top of his head. He is still a young man, and though his hair is not "silvered," his skull is; thus differing from many men and women, who have no silver on their brain, but a large supply of it in their hair. People turn grey much earlier in life than formerly. Such being the case, it is surprising that they do not take better care of it. The hair is a vegetable, and may be cultivated, its growth strength- ened, and its texture improved by care, attention, and the aoplication of the proper fertilizing sproperties. That this is the case has been amply demonstrated, and ;therefore no one need have thin or grey hair, or a coarse and wiry stubble. provided they will use the proper care. Toe preparation most in vogue for this purpose, is undoubtedly Mrs. S. A. Alien's World's Hair Restorer, which never fails of arresting the fall- ingout of tSts hair, or restoring grey hair to 14 original colour, strength, and glossy luxuriance. It is besides the most delicate and delightful hair dressing in the world. It may be purchased of any chemist or perfumer, in any town or city. (327.).

div.p: _CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSI )NS.

The June General Quarter Sessions were oPenedi at Chester Castle on Monday, before Lord Egerton,. of Tatton (chairman), and his Honour Judge Hora- tia Lloyd (deputy chairman.) The County business was transacted in a magistrates' room, Lord Eger— ton presiding. The chief constable of the county, Colonel Hamersley, submitted a return of crime for the previous quarter, which gave a total of 2,293' apprehended and summoned, of whom 35 were committed for trial, 1,955. summarily convicted, and 303 discharged. During the same quarter 490 males and 98 females were proceeded against for drun- kenness, and 525 males and 71 females in the col- responding period of last year, there thus being an increase of 27 cases of female drunkenness, and a decrease of 26 cases of male drunkenness. In the preceding quarter there was a decrease of 16 males and an increase of 26 females charged with this offence. Amongst the return of local police rates required for the quarter com- mencing Ist October next are mentioned the Altrincham police division at a quarter of a penny, estimated to produce £426 ss, and the Runcorn police division at I (It a penny, estimated to produce £322 Ms 10d. The re- port of the county analyst, Mr. J. Caster Bell, stated I that during the quarter ending June 30th he had analysed 117 samples. Amongst them were 15 from the Altrincham district, and 8 from the Runcorn district. Two samples of milk received from the Altrincham and Northwich Divisions were so poor as to bring them under the Adulteration Act. Only three samples of water had been sent in during the quarter, one from the Runcorn Authority and two I from the W arrington Rural Sanitary Authority, and only one was a good sample. At a subsequent meeting of the Contagious Diseases Committee, the Chief Constable, in addition to other matters, re- ported that two animals had been attacked with pleuro-pneumonia, one belonging to Mr. Boardman, at Grappenhall, on the sth of April, and the other, belonging to Mr. Bradford, in the same township. Both the cows were slaughtered, together with a healthy bull, which had been in contact with the affected animal on the latter's premises. Mr. Board- man's premises were 56 days free from the disease on the. Ist inst., and Mr. Rradford's on the 15th inst., and the Chief Constable suggested that the area pre- scribed in this district as infected with pleuro- pneumonia be declared free. In the Altrincham division ten animals had been attacked with rabies, of which eight had been killed, and two had died. Since the last report 22' swine and 2 sheep had been attacked with anthrak at Messrs. Percival's, Aston; 24 died, 2 were killed, and 3 recovered—including the live remaining under treatment on the 2nd April last. -
FOOTPATH DISPUTE AT RAINFORD.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. Thomas Pilkington and Alderman 3. C. Gamble, Mr. Thomas Boardinam. farmer, Rainford, was sum- moned for trespassing on the London and North- Western Railway, near Rainford Station, and after warning had been given him not to do so by the company's servants, on April 22nd' and May 12th. Mr. Preston. appeared for the railway company, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. The ground upon which defendant was charged with trespassing had been substituted by people for an old footpath which the company had closed, andwhich led from the end of the ilatform across the rails to a footpath which connected Rushy-lane and Ormskirk-road. Mr. Preston said the Railway company had not entered into those proceedings with any., feelings to- wards Mr. Boardman, and he would be satisfied with an expression of feeling from, the bench and a small penalty.—Mr. Pinhey, surveyor; put in a plan, and in cross-examination said he did not know that as often as the railway company built a wall across the footpath iniquestion the public pulled it down. The might be used by a great number of people. pathway Hehad heard that people' insisted upon going along the footpath, and that they went through a hole in the wall when the gate was locked.—John Riley, stationmaster, said the wall had been thrown down only once teals knowledge in the last eight years. There waa a notice board • warning trespassers. When he. went to the station, eight years ago, people went through the wall night and day, and be did not try to stop them. He could' not say it was a public highway.—Joseph Jackson,:who hau known the place since 1858, said, the footpath went alongside tho' Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, and on their property all the way, and not on the London and North-' Western Company's property at all. Cross- examined: He could not say how many times the London and North-Western Company's wall had •been pulled down; liople knocked it down so often i and people went in spite of the notice-boards. —Thomas Beesley said he warned defendant, who replied that it had been a road for years, and the company could not stop him, He refused to go, back.—Cross-examined; On the 22nd April sixty- nine persons crossed. . The majority. were colliers, and they asserted that they had a right to Use the road:—Mr. Swift submitted that Mr. Preston had put himself out of court. It did not matter what Acts of Parliament the railwayconipanies had, because any and every Act of Parliament relating to trespass was subject to the, ordinazy rule of law. A bona fide claim of right was raised, and the juris- diction of the coUrt was ousted. He (Mr. Swift) had a very large number ofold inhabitants of Rain- ford in attendance who thought they were right in, maintaining the path.—The magistrates thought Mr. Roardman had reasonable right to suppose that the path was public; and therefore it was a case for a civil court. The eases were dismissed.
