"THE STABILITY OF OUR TIMES." On Sunday evening a Jubilee service was held in St. John's Presbyterian Church, Warrington, at which the sermon was preached by the Rev. J. Warnock, pastor, the subject being "The stability of our times." The reverend gentleman selected as his text Isaiah xxxiii, 6. In the course of his re- marks'he said that in an endeavour to bring before his hearers some thoughts suggested by the- great national celebration of the past week it vrae not inappropriate to point out—though it might be but briefly and imperfectly—wherein lay its moral, and religious significance. It was indeed no incon- siderable advantage to he derived from such an event if it did nothing more than gain a we 11%.. earned holiday for the'sons and daughters of toil,. and bind together in closer bonds of aympathy and fellow-ship the different classes which composed' the community; but there when° necessity, in the nature of things, why their gains, should be all of a temporal and social kind. To these who believed in an overruling Providence no event occurred causeless; and if every event had thus a spiritual- as well as a temporal aspect, they might well be- lieve that there was peculiarsignificancein, an event which exercised more or less influence on the wel- fare of so many millions of mankind: If asked to characterize in a single word the reason why they should commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Queen's accession to the throne he would say— Because it is a marvellous illtistration of the stability, of the security which' charac- terizes the nation. In a natio*: "whose flag had braved a thousand -years the battle and: the breeze' there must have been manycriticalmoments when its destiny—or even its very, existence,. as it were—hung in the balance; but musuch. critical experiences, no such dangerous moments had' oc- curred in their day. Since the beginning of ' the present century Mere had not been any attempt made by any foreign nation' to. invadeour shores* while during the• same period there had been an entire' absence of those • internal fendi which, in former centuries did so much to• imperil' the nation's safety and impair• her strength. Now, remembering: that tho chief: end+ of civil' government was to- protect life- and property,. it must be confessed that whatever errors or faults might have been committed on the part of our rulers, still the functions of grivernment had, for the last fifty years at any rate, been performed exceedingly well. Of course, it would neither be true nor jast to say that all this had been brought about by the sovereign lady who sat at the bead of this great empire, for her greatness, in so far as sovereignty was concerned, was neither more nor less than the greatness of, the people over whom she reigns. The wealth and resources of the nation were due, under God, to the wisdom of 'oar people and the wisdom of the statesmen who had from time to time carried on the business of the State. But candour was also cbliged to acknowledge that the Queen had per.formed the duties of her high station with singular dili- gence, wisdom, and discretion ; so that owing to her many virtues it became easy fOr us to be "in subjection to the powers that be." He was far from saying that the British conntaution was perfect in all its details, or that it would not have to undergo ,further modifications to suit new emergencies; but it was perhaps not too much to say regarding it that by a marvellous blending together of or- der and liberty it served its purpese as well—nay, better-- than any other the world had ever seen. From the earliest times writer.' on political' philosophy had been accustomed to mention three essentially distinct forms of government —monarchy, in which power is vested in the hand of a sin- gle ruler ; aristocracy, in which power is vested in the hands of the best or most capable citizens ; while demo- cracy gave equal rights and equal power to all the people. As a matter of fact, the British constitution did not consist of any one of these forms of government, but was a com- bination of them all. The advantage of such a combina- tion was well known to ancient writers, though it was cer- tain that the idea never had such a realization as it had in our day. The Sovereign at the head of the State gave unity and permanence to the execrative power. Our legis- lators, or the larger portion of them were chosen because of their special Ltness for their position; while political power was in the last resource reaognised as lying—where it actually does lie, as a matter ot fact—among the masses- of the people. There wee doubtless manifest wisdom in soeh an arrangement; it had been arrived at through the conflict and experience of centuries, and it was because he believed that it was a, fair interpretation of the facts of, human nature, in its social aspect that he thought it gave good hope of permanency in the time to come. Another ele- ment of national stability was. the general diffusion of ' knowledge among the masses of the people. Looked at simply as a question of statesmanship, there could be no doubt that the money spent on elementary education was a good investment: The education of the people of this country even fifty years ago was irt a deplorable condition; but they could notbe too thankful now that a nation which spent SOMA 120 millions a year in intoxicating liquors had also seen fit to give three and a half millions to help on the much-needed work of the educatiot of the country. Another element in the stability of our times was the increased zeal and activity which characterizes the various branches of the Christian Church, and there could be no doubt that; as regards religious activity, the present times were better than the former. Remarkable advances-had been made in bibli- cal scholarahip..and for his own part he believed that the revision of the English bible was likely to be the most re- markable event in the Queen's reign—an event which would, be had in remembrance when many other changes which they now valued would be buried in forgetfulness. tier Majesty's long reign of 50 years seemed to be an epitome of national stability. One felt in it a sense of security. It told them, in no doubtful way, that' they were happily free from those sudden and violent changes which were se often, atieoded with harm and lose. Re-thought the Queen bade done not a little to further the inMrests of the nation, be-- cause she had kept so c,osely in touch with the welfare eft the people; and her influence had always been favourable to the advancement of religion and morality.—After the sermon two verses+ of the NationaltAtithem were sung by thee choir and congregation.
JUINIAE SETMON AT WARRINGION

• - • PARISH CHURCH.. A Jubilee service was held at Warrington Parish Church on Sunday morning, when an eloquent ser- mon was preached by the Ven. Archdeacon of War- rington, to a crowded congregation. The May& (Alderman Pickmere) and the following members of the Town Council formed in procession` at the Town Hall soon after ten o'clock and procended to church, ;—Aldersaen Burgess, Chandley, Davies, Holmes,. Sutton, and Webster; and Councillors Ashton.. Barker, Brown, Dakin, Dixon, Francomb, Heaton, Hutchinson, Jolley, Marsh, John Pierpoint, Platt, Joseph Taylor, Tinsley, and John E. Wright. There were also in the procession a number of the ! members of the Borough Police' Porce, under the I direction of Chief Constable Hunt and Inspectors- Spinks and Cox; the members of the Fire Brigade, under the charge of Superintendent Prank Turner; the town clerk (Mr. Brook), the borough treasurer (Mr. Chorley), the deputy town clerk (Mr. Whittle), an& the following gentlemen :—Messrs. Thomas Morrie, Thomas- Robinson, William Bennett, John Ileshath, James, Smethurst,. Thomas Jones, and others. At church, prayers were read' by the Rev. T. 11. Twist, the lessons by the Rev. E. J..Wihrocks, whithrthe communion service was taken by the Revs: J. A. Drummond and J. J. Laughlin'.• An anthem, was sung, the solo being takbir by Mr. R. Pairclough. Mr. WA Woods was at the organ. The AnCIIDEACON„ who preached from the words, "What mean ye by 'dile service," Exodus 12-26, in the course of his sermon said that millions of voices I spoke thelanguage oV grateful Englishmen, when I they declared at this time-That God bad blessed them, blessed their nation, blessed their countryp and blessed their Queen. Bin why this'-joy? It was- because they at this time commemorated the 50) , years' reign of her who represented the Royal house. they so dearikloved ; and they thanked Almighty God as well for' what the Queen was net as for what, she was. She-might have been guilty of the- in.• trigues of a paitizan ; she might have fanned the flame of humairpassion from one end ofithe country!' to the other by taking either side of the great)- schools of political life whien represented in their totality the whole moral andl intellectual. !strength' of the nation; or she might have been) tolerant' to luxurious vice which somehow or other skulked, about some of the courts in-Europe even at the pre- - sent time, but " hereourt -Was pisre, her life serene." Then they thanked God for whist she was and had been—the centre of national sympathy, the expres- sion of the national heart, the maiden, the wife, the mother, the widow. There wae one grand charac- teristic amongst others of our Queen. It was not interference with national rights, not the abridg- ment of national liberty, but the assertion of a woman's mighty love. Was there a calamity qn a large-scale she had not shown her interest in? Was there a sorrow she had not in a measure en- deavoured to solace? Did an explosion in a mine. cause -widows and orphans to multiply in her great I centres-of enterprise? If so the Queen sent her message of tenderness and compassion. Was there a shipwreck? Was there a disaster hY flood or field? She was again ready to show that while high on the • throne of this world' e power, she was still* higher inthe aptitude and expression of woman's sympathy. She had realized the dream of the ancients, who used to speak of their rulers as " the fathers of the nation." Abundantblessings had been directlyananifested in the gifts of God to this nation. There was first the wonderful blessing of the. moral advancement of this great people, in the sphere of law and the ; sphere of.love. Never before had there been such development of law in the interest of the tender, the weak and! the frail, as in the Victorian era. That era would be marked as the era -when it was, no longer possible for women and children to toil in mines, as the era which enabled Lard Shaftes- bury to perfect the work begun by Sirßobert Peel, . as the erain which the wages of the working classes had-increased and them hours of labour had diminished,,as the era in which the bible was re- . vised, analsthe penny testament was first issued,' and as the era when the whole wide world seemed to be approaching that great time when " the knowledge of the lord shalt 'cover the earth as,the, waters cover the sea." What should, he say of scientific investigation? • They ,had en- girdled the earth with the language of fire; they had imprisoned! the very sun. to makeit take the likness of thosethey loved; they had pressed pho- tography into the interests of friendship and jastice ;; they read the very spots on thedisc of the" sun, and from these they couldctell the material of which it was composed; while electricity had been pressed into the service of the healing art. Owing, to the blessed advancement in sanitation, they be- earae more' and'more acquainted) with the influ-ence of., light and air and water and the like upon longevity; aind,,in spite of the- rate at which we were new • livingolon the whole the Victorian era would be marked as one during which the average length of human life-was increased and .Ideveloped. What should he say ohmaterial progress?' Men of every clime, and latitudet.and longitude do- lighted to speak of the Queen as-their sovereign, and all I this meant material advancement. But for the Queen's sense-el God as a maiden, a wife, and a mother, he believed that the court and the country and tile colonies, would be in a fardifferent position, to the one they-occupied now. The Queen's exam- ple, her religion;, and her sense of God, which had ; , permeated all, classes of society, had been abun- dantly blessed to those over whom God had cello& her torule. England as a nation would yet rise higher if they kept that sense of God. To do that- became an individual matter, and therefore he would plead with every one to "make- his calling and ele3-- tion sure."

PENKETH ORA/NM:IE.—The minatee of a meeting of the Penketh Parochial Committee were read. They stated that Mr. Routledge had produced and eiplained a plan and sec- tion of the proposed alternative drainage scheme fcathe township, and, it was agreed by the committee that the plan and section be approved and submitted to the Local Govern- ment Board after the approval °fettle Rural Sanitary Author- itv.—The SUNVEYOR said he had had submitted to him by the clerk the plan prepared by Mr. J. C. Routledge, I man of the Penketh Parochial. Committee, for a proposed intercepting drain, by which the pollution of the brook would he largely prevented, and he bad been requested to report upon it. The plan proposes a new sewer to be laid on the north side of the brook for a length of about 830 yards, and then, as the brook turns near Penketh Hall and runs south, it proposes a new. sewer in •continuation of the other on the east side of the brook for a lengthael about 420 yards, and then emptyingtinto the brook where the cul- vert carries it under the railway and canal at the Penkethr Hall ceossing. This sewer would intercept the bulk ce:', the drainage of Penketh, and as it is a part of the complete scheme which be submitted to the Authority ira,lBB3, and for which Penketh is not vet ripe, he should give it a general approval, but going into matters ore detail be thought the plan should be teferred back to the Parochial Committee for further consideration on the following points: —First-, the introduction of, more manholes in the sewer, and the sewer to be run in straight lengths from manhole to manhole for the purposeef readily cleansicg and for ven- tilation. The average distance apart on the, plan is about 400 yards. Second, the manholes not trr hale the bottoms lower than the sewer, as shown, as' this feems thenvinto , cesspools, a system now condemned by sanitary engiaeors ; and, third, when the sewer as shown would empty into the brook after intercepting the sewage, the water and sewage would pass together through the culvert ander the railway and canal, and coming afterwards into. the opens before reaching the river, these polluted waters. would he used by cattle for drinking, which should be ayi.ided if poseible. It is probable %rich of these points has already received the. COUSideration of the committee, but as he had no report be- fore him, he could not say wNether thie, was to. It was also probable that the additional expens.s that would be incurred in giving attention to the first and third points might be urged against their being undertaken at once, bot I as difficalsies might arise through their not receiving atten- tion it would be well for the committee, if in any way pos- sible, to grapple-with them at the. commencement and pre- pare for overcoming them even if the additional works were not at once carried out. The fall in the proposed sewer is very little, but appears to be as much as can be get from the lavele of the land and brook. No estimate of cost had been, laid before him, so on this he had said nothing, the, question now being simply whether the plan should go for- ward for the consideration of She Local Crovernment Board. __The CLEE said he had received another letter from the Local Government Jitoard pressing for the plan ; he thought it was the fourth letter they had sent —Ube SURVNYOR thought that if the plan was sent as it was at present it would be sent back by the Local Governm ,nt Boaid,—Mr. OW i EN moved that n accordance with the suggestion of the Surveyor, the plan be returned to the Parochial Committee, together with the report of the Surveyor —Mr. JoLLey seconded this proposal, which was aereed to. Ngsr ButuANGe —The SURVEYOR reported that during tha month inspection bad been made of the followinv build- ings :—Mr Millington, s houses, Penketh ; the Wesleyan Schools, Penketh ; the Church Sunday Schools, Sankey ; Dr Gornall's house, Grappenhall ; Mr Smith's house, Grap- penhall ; Mr Bramliall'a houses, Latchford ; Messrs Craik land Taylor's houses, Padgate; and Mr MounfiAd's houses, Padgate.—The report. was adopted. This was the principal business before the Committee.

WIT AND HUMOUR. A girl may be speaking the truth when she says: "Well, I like that fellow's impudence." What in a woman is called "'curiosity," in a man is grandiloquently magnified into the" spirit of inquiry." "A seaman washed overboard," exclaimed Mrs. Fangle as she read a newspaper head-line; "but he perhaps was so dirty they hadn't enough water on the'ship." "What is usually the nationality of a boot-black my dear?" asked' Mrs. Caution of her husband. "Oh, it varies!" replied Caution. "Sometimed they are Polish and sometimes Shinese." "The friction of an insurance policy on unproductive property" is the latest reason given for a good many fires in flour mills. An Alderney cow swallowed a sovereign several years ago and the coinwas recently discovered in her:storoach after she was butchered. Her owner often Wondered what made her milk so rich. A lady of charitable disposition asked 'a tramp if she could not assist him by mending his clothes: "Yes, madaln," he said, "I have a button, and if you will sew a shirt on it I will be greatly obliged." "And so you would hke to know what the M.D.' after a doctor's name means, Edith, would you, dear? Well, it is pnly an indication that he possesses a license to kill, the letters referred to standing for May Destroy'!" Prohibition in Georgia is said to have developed a liquor flask with a:cover made to look like a book. And; like a book, its Contents are 'frequently red—which " maketh a full man." ' "Judge, what is the best substitute for wisdom?" asked a loquacious lawyer. "Suppose you try silence," responded the judge. Topers will patroniae a bar; from place to place they mope; the best bar they could patronize would be a bar of soap. Young suitor: "Will you promise to be mine?" Belle: "I can't say now; give me a week to answer." He gave her a week to answer, and she immediately hires a detec- tive to find out what his prospects are. "I must congratulate you on your marriage, Mr. Pugs- by. Your wife is a charming woman." "She is indeed —loving, amiable and accomplished, and so easily pleased.' "Oh, I amiable, that when I heard that she was about to marry you!" MORE MEANT THAN MET THI3 EAR.—A certain West Indian judge was' not remarkable for sagacity, on the bench. At an official ball he criticised the waltzing of a witty member of the Bar. " Ah, my friend, you are a bad waltzer!" " Ah, but you are a bad judge, was the rejoinder. A MAN OF linsonacus.—Once there was a hired man who was constantly astonishing his employer, a farmer. One day the farmer went into the barn and found that his man had hanged himself. Looking at the dangling body a few minutes he exclaimed: "What on earth will that fellow do next?" Swam, Bur GREAT.—Scene—School not a hundred miles from Edinburgh. Time—General Election 1880. Her Majesty's inspector, examining: "What IS the most famous town' my boy?" Small boy: "Please sir, Galashiels." 'Her Majesty's inspector: "And why is Galashiels the most famous town, my boy?" Small boy, after thinking: "Please, sir, Gladstone gets his breeks there!" . - Mix.—A recent advertisement contains the follow- ing,—" If the gentleman who keeps the boot shop WA the red head will return the umbrella of a young lady with whalebone ribs and an iron handle to a slate roofed grocer's shop he will hear something to his advantage as the same is the gift of a deceased mother now no more with the name engraved on it." Some years ago a delegate from France to the Free Church of Scotland Assembly who had not acquired the English language very perfectly, observing that a bare country was called a barren one in England, remarked on rising, as he looked round on the great number of bald heads and venerable men before him, that he felt "much embarrassed in speaking before so many barren

,heads." _ _ They were a newly-married Irish couple, and; the "better half "being iii, the husband did the cooking. Said Barney," Och, Biddy, dear, I've boiled a nice pet of praties ! But I'm afeared there's• somethiif the matther wid em! Whin' I put thim into the watther they had beautiful whoite eyes' an', now that they're out, they're black wans !" Said Biddy—in bed, enjoy- ing Barney's dilemma—" Barney, Barney, ye haven't put enough salt in the watther to kill em, an' they've been fightin" wid wan another I" REGULATING THE Otoce—Sandy Neil was beadle, bell- ringer, and gravedigger in a certain small parish in the neighbourhood of Lanark. The kirk clock was rather eccentric Mite movements, anddid net keep time. Sandy took it in hand, and tinder his care it kept splendid time. Tam Scot, meeting him one day on the road, said, "Man, Sandy, the clock does brawly noo ; hoo div ye manage her ? ' "Wool," rejoined Sandy," when she gangs ewer fast I just pitch a shulefu' o' gravel into her, and when she gangs slow I just take a piekle oot." HE WASN'T COLOUR-BLIND—ONLY OTHER BLIND.—One day lately a stalwart grenadier was standing at the cor- ner of Regent-street, when a gentleman evidently some- what the worse for liquor approached him with unsteady footsteps. In his right hand he held a letter, and with this he made several thrusts at the soldier's expansive chest. The latter, resenting what he deemed an insult to the scarlet cloth that he wore, sent the gentleman sprawling. "Confounded `shame o' these Femansh," re- plied the fallen one, "to go an' put infernal machinsh in the pillar boxshes, mutilatin' lot 'f innoshent people!" ABOUT Kresnaa.—A physician says that tuberculosis, diptheria, and infectious fevers are all possible or actual results of kissing. The worst disease contracted by the young man who devotes several nights a week to the labial exercise is palpitation of the heart, which fre- quently terminates in a violent case of matrimony. That is less dangerous but more expensive than either tuberculosis or diphtheria. And it hangs on much longer, too. DRINKING DODGES OUT WEST.—A man sat On a salt barrel on Michigan Grand Avenue, making a great dis- play of eating a raw carrot. A small coloured boy halted in front of him, watched the performance for a while and then said: "My fadder tried dat dodge on de odder day." "What dodge?" "Tryin' fur to git sync:- pathy, but itdidrft work.' "Why ?" "Case de whisky smells right frevi de carrot. He's tryin, onions now." I AWKWARD IGKING.—A gentleman of birth, while prac- tising pennianship one day, wrote his name upon a blank slip of paper, and allowed it to lie on his desk. It • attracted the attention of aneihbour, who for a joke filled in the space above the signature in the form of a promissory note; and a few days afterwavds the joking neighbour presented the paper, with an offer to allow considerable discount if the apparent drawer would clash it at the time. The gentleman perceived the joke, and the holder of the document, placing it in his pocket, departed, and nothing more was said about it. Subse- quently the holder was stricken with paralysis and died, and his executers, finding the note, and having no know- ledge of the joke attached to it, brought ait, and re- covered the sum for which it was drawn. The joker had meant no harm, but he, as well as his friend, had been careless, and someone had to pay the penalty. AMATEUR Cowinnino.—A gentleman took an unopened bottle of champagne from a table, and offered bets to any amount—small ones for preference, as the trick was admittedly a" sell "—that he would drink a glass of champagne out of that particularbottle without drawing or piercing the cork, without cawing it to be drawn or. pierced, and without breaking or in any way injuring the bottle. The utter, impossibility of accomplishing such a thing might have induced the incautious to bet : against it being done; thereupon the holder simply turned it upside down, poured a glass of ehatnpagne into the hollow at the bottom, andkundoubtedly drank it from and out of the bottle. A MESSAGE OF IMPORTANCE:4n a certain village in Maryland a small boyllicked up a breeze in the parish church one Sunday. it seems that a certain good *roman bought a calf's head and put it on to boiLleaving her little boy to mind it while she went to church close by. The minister had ,reached his" Fifthly, my bre- thnn," when a small boy•stuck his head in the door and 'whispered," Mammal" The good iwoman recognised • her son instantly, and began at once to make signs to him to leave the door. • "Mamma!" again came the whisper—this time a little 'louder than before. The mother shook her finger at the boy warningly, and in- dulged in other familiar ,pantomime with which she was accustomed to awe her son. 13.ut it didn't work worth a cent. The boy•was excited and in deadearnest. Raising his voice, he shouted, "Mamma, you needn't wink and blink et me; but you had better come kerne right away, for the calf's head is buttin' all the dumplins out of the pot."

On her way from Paddington to the Palace Her Majesty received an address of congratulation on ter Jubi- lee from the inhabitants of Kensington. div.head: "SAM' OUT."
div.p: "SAM' OUT."

[Sir Gilbert Greenall was accidentally shut out, from voting for the Government, en Monday night, in favour of making the Coercion Bill permanent.] 'Shut out," but "accidentally," mark that, friends; The spirit willing, but the flesh was weak. He is not quite so nimble as he was, And cannot dance attendance on the " Whip " As in old days, when ready vote was given For backing Church Rates, and the Irish Church, Although the people's voice cried—" Down with both!" There was a time when he rushed gladly in 'T. swell the Tory bigots' party cry 'Gainst Monast'ries and Convents; and, besides, lie voted 'gainst the Sunday Closing Bill. And Flogging in the Army—did he not • Go in for lashing, ay, and many stripes? Who shall dare hint, then, that he hesitates At a Coercion Bill to last for aye? "Eternal torment," there, now, that's the thing; Punish 'em ever, and let 'em have it hot. They're Irishmen; they're simply Hottentots, As Salisbury says, and isn't that enough? Trample upon them, huddle them in gaol, Crush, fetter them, or drive them from the land. And then, egad !--and there's the fun of it— We'll talk of liberty and equal laws. No, no, you'll never see the Brewer shirk, When the poor Irishman is on the rack; But, still, with weight of years upon his back, He is not quite as quick when the 41, hip calls; The spirit's willing, but the flesh is weak "Shut out;" yes, yes; it was an accident; These things will happen with the best machine. But don't forget he is a true-blue Tory ; A trifle fossilised, but—anti-Irish.

WINDSOR ROYAL CASTLE.

With' each copy of "The Examiner" of this week we present our readers with an engraving of the great Royal Castle of Windsor to which the Queen retired after the memorable celebration of the jubilee ot her reign in London last week. The sketch is executed from an original drawing of Windsor Castle, the point of view being the bank of the Thames, and it presents what is considered the most imposing and completest view of the var- ious and picturesquely-grouped features of this !majestic seat of the Royal. House of England. Since the Norman conquest Windsor castle has been the home of royalty, and in its clustering towers, its bastions and facades, its chapels and halls, its vaults and cloisters, its quadrangles and terraces, it strikes the fancy as an epitome in stone of the story of the Monarchy in England whose prosperous periods have each been marked by im- •portant and characteristic structural additions to and embellishments of this noble castle-palace. Thus we read that William of Normandy, soon after he had conquered England, and placed the crown of Edward the Confessor upon his own head, cast a covetous eye upon the sunny eminence by the Thames at Windsor, and proposed an exchange of the estate of which it formed a part by the Ab- bot and Convent of St. Peter at Westminster, to whom it belonged, for certain other land which the Norman had appropriated in Essex; and thereupon he erected a castle on the hill, emparked the estate, and extended the boundaries of the Windsor Forest. About thirty years after Henry the First enlarged, and for the most part rebuilt the Castle, and sur- rounded it with a massive wall. The succeeding Kings, Stephen, the second Henry, who built some of its towers, the first Richard and John, in turn dwelt here, and the last-named stood a siege in the Castle by his rebellious barons in 1216. The wife of Edward the First, Queen Eleanor, made Windsor her favourite residence. Edward the Second also sojourned there in peaceful times, and his son, the brave Edward-the Third, was born within its wall. He was so fond of the spot that, when he became King, he undertook to rebuild the Castle on a grand scale. The works were prosecuted with energy during the greater part of twenty-five years, from 1350 to 1375. After the lapse of nearly a century, Edward the Fourth extended the build- ings, and erected St. George's Chapel. Next, Henry the Seventh had the roof of the chapel richly vaulted, and erected important structures in the upper Ward; and his successor, Henry the Eighth, rebuilt the great gateway in the lower Ward. Some improvements Were made during the reigns of Edward VI. and Mary I.; and then Elizabeth, who frequented Windsor much during her long reign, built the fine terrace on the north front. Charles , the First, too, made some additions, among them a ; gateway leading to the Park, and, after he fell into I the hands of his enemies, was for a time confined iii the Castle. Charles the Second repaired and beau- tified the whole of the Castle buildings; he likewise continued the terrace round the east and south sides of the upper Court. During the last two hun- dred years almost every sovereign has expended somewhat upon the embellishment of the Cas- tle, but the most costly and conspicuous of the modern extensions have been those carried out under the commands of George the Third, 'George the Fourth, and Queen Victoria. The fea- tures of boldness and strength in the exterior of the Castle. which impart to it an air of domination and an aspect of fortress-like security, belong to the ancient periods of its design, the work of its Nor- man and Plantagenet founders; whilst many of the internal ;adornments which express the highest re- finement and modern palatial comfort and splen- dour, and artistic taste, are the contributions ot the present and the immediately precedent reigns. 'The Queen's stateliest home, in fact, is a good em- blem, in its combination of antique puissance, with graceful lightness and richness in its later modifications, of its illustrious mistress, who, al- though the descendant and I.leir of a long line of martial and semi-barbaric kings, and representing the oldest surviving monarchy in Europe, is yet in her own person the perfect lady, not only sovereign of a mighty realm and a proud people, but mistress of every rare accomplish- ment, and discriminating patroness of every beauti- ful art. The plan of the Castle consists of two courts, known as the upper and lower wards, be- tween which, standing on an artificial mound, the highest ground of the site is the familiar Round Tower. Our engraving displays this lordly tower, conspicuous in the midst of the Castle fabrics, with the royal standard floating above the turret.which springs from its roof on the south side. A striking landscape stretching away into twelve counties is beheld from the summit of this tower. The terraced walks which pass round the upper ward of the castle afford a delightful promenade, and command the most charming landscapes and vistas across the wooded expanse and down the avenues of Windsor Great Park and the Home Park. Ancient Windsor Forest, out of which these parks an other enclosures of the Royal demesne have been constituted, embraced a circumference of seventy-seven miles. Much of the land was for- merly waste, of the nature of bog, swamp; or brake; but it has been industriously reclaimed and im- proved until every trace of its primitive wildness and roughness has disappeared. The English people may properly be proud of Windsor Castle, which attests the solidity and the duration of the national nstitutions, the glory of England's state centuries .since, and its unsurpassed wealth, renown, and material greatness to-day.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THUBSDAX.

The House of Commons has returned this week to the Coercion Bill, which it is curtly announced will be carried through the Report • Stage at seven o'clock precisely on Monday. As far as prac- tical purposes are concerned, this edict might as well have been put in force last Monday, after the division on Mr John Morley's amendment, limiting the term of the Act to three years. There was a well sustained debate on this point, in which Mr. Gladstone took part. But with that stand the Li- beral leaders have been content, and have practi- cally refrained from taking further part in the controversy. The Parnellites take another view of their duty. They are determined to bring into strong light the peculiar means by which this mon- strous Bill is forced upon the people of Ireland. They will so arrange matters that when legislative coercion comes into effect at the hour named in Monday, there will remain a large proportion of the amendments which have not even gone through the form of discussion. They will be able to say of the Act that it was added to the Statute Book by physical force, and not through the ordinary process i of debate. It will be a barren victory, and n Be- miring it the Irish members make the House of Commons an exceedingly uninteresting place. The real interest in politics is centred outside the House of Commons. It is fixed to-day, as it has been throughout the year, upon the attitude of the Dissentient Liberals, vis-a-via the Tories on the one , hand and the Liberal party on the other. The event of this week is the publication of the letters in which Sir George Trevelyan and Mr. Chamberlain address the public. The anger created in the Dis- sentient cqmp by the letter of Sir George Trevelyan, marks the measure of its importance. It is but a few months since Sir George was the cherished colleague of Mr. Chamberlain, and one of the idols of the 'Times." Sir George, who, as even his bitter adversaries admit, is above all things a fair-minded man, has recognised the altered position taken up by Mr. Gladstone since the introduction of his fam- ous bill, and is now ready to assist in trying once more to deal with the problem of Home Rule for Ireland. Above all he declines to work with the Tory Government in order to prolong Mr. Glad- stone's exclusion from power. That is 'the unpar- donable sin, and Mr. Chamberlain attacks him in a querulous epistle, useful only as showing how hot is his anger. The immediate effect of Sir George Trevelyan's return to the fold has been to widen the gap between the Dissentient Liberals and the main body of the party. Mr. Chamberlain is just now en- tranced by the notion of creating a new party, to be called" the National party," which is to carry every- thing before it. Lord R. Churchill is working with him in this endeavour, which Lord Hartington in his passive manner approves. "The Party," when it is created, may develop many principles. Its sus- taining one in its present inchoate form is to keep out Mr. Gladstone.

The last lingering hope that the Queen would in some Royal manner make personal acknowledgment of the unprecedented prosperity enjoyed for fifty 3-ears has now been finally dispelled.. Acknow- ledgment has been made. But it has taken the simple, and not expensive, form of a letter of thanks addressed to the Home Secretary. Whether the expectation that the Queen would do something handsome was justified or not may be a question. But there is no question that it widely existed. Very little has been said in the newspapers, partly from a desire not'to be hasty in commenting upon a matter that might arrange itself any day, but largely from a commendable desire not to take a course that might appear censorious towards royalty. ,How extensively the matter has been talked of in privaie circles the experience of every reader will bear testimony. The general idea was that, owing to circumstances and force of habit, the Queen had not seen her way to spend through suc- cessive years the full amount of money allotted for Royal purposes out of the National purse. Here was a rare oppor- tunity of gracefully squaring the balance. A principal feature of the Jubilee has been the touting for money. The private and even the official purse has been drawn upon in all directions, from the Imperialilnstitute to the Church House; from the noble object of the relief of hospitals down to the equally commendable effort to give children a holiday or old ladies a tea. Everyone has in degree given something in token of joy that the Queen has been privileged to live and enjoy the ad- vantages of her high position for half a century. This was well enough and nice enough. But to tell the honest truth, it has been a little chilling to find that the personage who has been the principal re- cipient of the accumulated advantages celebrated should be content tn make acknowledgment in a Simple letter. Ido not say whether this feeling is justifiable or not; I am merely recording the fact of its widespread existence.

_ On Monday evening the Viscountess Kawase gave a party "to meet his Imperial Highness Prince Komatsu." Who, is the Viscountess and who the Prince, may reasonably be asked. Well, the Viscoun- tess is the wife of the Japanese Minister at the Court of St. James's, and the Prince is the heir ap- parent to the throne of Japan. It is an odd circum- stance, strikingly illustrative of the predominant proclivities of the Japaqese Government, that they have within the last few years adopted European titles for their magnates. The Chancellor and Foreign Secretary were four years ago known as plain "Mr." Now they are both counts, and the Imperial Minister at this court is a viscount. These are paltry titles compared with the ancient orders of Japan. But Japan is nothing if not modern and western, and so its old nobility are giving place to counts and viscounts. Prince Komatsu was not at the party on Monday night, having been "com- manded," at twenty-four hours' notice, to dine with ' the Queen at Windsor. But there was, notwith- standing. a brilliant company, a little too crowded for the rooms in Cavendish-square. :.Among the ladies present was the Queen of Hawaii, a buxom dame verging on fifty, I should say. Her Majesty's complexion is of. a rich brown, quite distinct from the negro type, and pleasant to look upon. She has a face full of humour, when she smiles reminding one curiously of Mr. Toole. She was splendidly dressed in ruby velvet robe,with a long train adorned with rich gold embroidery. It was pretty to see his Excellency the Japanese Minister taking her Majesty in to supper. His ignorance of the Hawaiian language was equalled, only by her darkness in all that con- cerned the Japanese tongue. But he bowed and smiled all the way to the supper table. She looked down upon him from her superior height, twitch- ing her massive lower lip, more than ever like Mr. Toole. The language of the supper table is a com- mon one. Her Majesty ate a jelly,'drank a bumper of champagne, and evidently enjoyed herself. There is little doubt that the new coinage "must go," as the Americans say, though there is a par- ticular circumstance connected with its creation that will make the process difficult. Poor Mr. Boehm comes in for a good deal of reproach in con- nection with the work. But it is no secret, it has been openly hinted at in the House of Commons by Mr. Geschen. that Mr. Boehm was not a free agent in the matter. It is, of all persons in the world, the Queen herself who has approved the grotesque medallion on the new coins. No description could do justice to the fatuity of the design. The bust represents a lady of uncertain age, with an ugly, long neck, and a mouth open in a helpless way that suggests libation, an effect strengthened by the tipsy way in which the crown is placeti askew on the head and looks as if it would presently slide down. It is said that the secret of the failure all lies in the drawing of the neck. The first sketch submitted to her Majesty was a pretty faithful like- ness; but she objected to the dumpy look about the neck, insisting that the Queen's neck was more , columnar, with the result of this comical carica-;

ture. These are objections taken upon artistic I grounds. There are other even more serious in the opening to fraud left by the unbusinesslike work. New half-sovereigns are everywhere looked upon with suspicion, lest one might entertain a gilded sixpence unawares. There is, in brief, not a good word to be said of th 7 new coinage from any point of view. In the Goupil gallery there are many visitors to see it collection of water-colour drawings of the Queen's Highland Home. Mr. Frederic Tucker has devoted himself to this subject, and so successfully as to explain the Queen's predilection for Balmoral. The Forest of Mar, with its lonely pass, almost mountain locked, its grey sky above, a few deer adding by their vicinity to the solitude of the scene, the stream winding along, fed by the rills that trickle down from the mountains—a picture like this should make the shares of the Great Northern Railway go up, and hurry Londoners out of town. Indeed tlie season promises to be unusually short. Henley and the cricket matches will end it, and the second week in July will witness the exodus.

FORMATION OF A NEW COUNTY POLICE D/ItISION.

On Tuesday afternoon a meeting of county magis- trates acting in the present St, Helens and Prescot police divisions, was held at Prescot to consider the formation of a new division, in consequence of the adoption of borough police in St. Helens. Mr, Gib- bon presided, and the Widnes magistrates present were Messrs. F. H. Gossage, H. S. Hall, J. Brook, T. S. Timmis, and H. W. Deacon. It was decided to , create a new division to be called "The Widnes Division," comprising the townships of Bold, Crou- ton, Ditton, Hale, Halewood, Rainhill, Speke, and Widnes. The acreage will be 22,832, and will be in charge of Superintendent Johnston (who for about nine years has been in St. Helens), assisted by In- , spector.Keighley (who has been in St. Helens about four years), and the force will consist of seven ser- geants and nearly forty constables. The Prescot division, which has hitherto included Wid- nes and several smaller townships, will com- prise Allerton Childwall, Croxteth, Eccleston (rural), HuytOn-cum-Roby, Knowsley, Prescot, Rainford, Tarbock, Wavertree, Whiston, Little Woolton, Much Woolton, and Windle (rural). The re-arranged Prescot division will continue under the supervision of Superinteneent Barker. Its acreage will be about 31,190, and it will be worked by a staff of two inspectors, eight sergeants and forty constables. St. Helens will cease to be a county police division, inasmuch as the townships of Bold, Ecclekon (rural), Windle (rural), and Rain- ford, which, with the borough, constituted the dis- trict, are merged into these two divisions. The new arrangement will, we understand, immediately come into operation.

Oa, FINANCIAL LETTER. IPROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT. .1 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The stock market during the past few dayshas been in a very fitful state, the primary cause being the uneasiness caused by the sudden panic and fall in New York, and the settle- ment which has occupied the chief attention of three days of the week. When the worst effects were considered at an end there came another bad shake in stocks, everything being more or less weak all round, and although the last prices are not the worst, the present condition of the market is very unsettled. Foreigners are perhaps less noticed at present, owing to the absence of any very disquieting news, and the great attention commauded by Americans. Home Rails have been very flat, the antici- pated increase in traffic, which was expected during the Jubilee week, not having come off. The result is that there has been a downward movement in most of the passenger Hoes. The one exception in Home Rails to the general fall is Hull and Barnsley, which have commanded a great amount of attention lately, due to the amalgamation scheme being near at band. Great firmness has been apparent in the money market during the past week, and there has been quite an active demand for money at double the rate of the preceding week. The charge fur the day to day loans is now 2 per cent, wLile at last settlement money was unlendable at per cent. The rise is due to the withdrawal of gold from the bank for New York and other quarters, notably Germany and South America, and still further withdrawals may be expected with the bank rate at 2 per cent. Country investors would do well to be cautioue in applying for shares of new com- panies, prbspectuses of which constantly reach them pri- vately. Several companies during the past few months have been stated gone to allotment, enly to be wound up with total loss to the shareholders. Two instances of companies being wound up will suffice. One, the directors went to allotment on a third of the capital necessary for obtaining possession of the pro- perty. In the other instance not a quarter of the necessary money for purchase was obtained, yet the directors went to allotment, and now both companies are to be wound up with loss to the unfortunate snarehelders, and profit only to the promoters, without any redress to the investor. That such a state of things should be allowed seems hardly cred- ible, and a bill is before Parliament to amend it, but, until it is, capitalists should be careful as to the companies they go into.withoet full inquiry.

Mr. Slug, M.P., is lying very ill at Sevenoaks. The news has created a good &al of anxiety at Burnley. The "Daily News" believes that the Government have finally resolved to abandon the bankruptcy provisions of the Irish Land Law Bill.
The " Morning Post" understands that on the third reading of the Irish Crimes Bill Mr. Gladstone intends to move the rejection of the measure.
A serious outbreak of swine fever has occurred at Gaws- worth, Cheshire. Twenty-two pigs have been condemned by the county veterinary inspector and slaw4htered.

, , . RETURN OF THE ROYAL PRINCES.—Prince Albert Victor and Prince George arrived in London on Friday morning from Dublin. The royal carriages were in waiting at Rostov Station, in which their Royal Highnesses drove to Marl- borough House.

A LONDON MYSTERY.—On Friday another human arm, evidently fellow to the one found on Thursday, was dis- covered in the Regent Canal, near the Midland Railway Station. It is believed the arm 'oolongs to the earns body of wnich the legs were also discovered on 'Thursday. All the limbs must have been cut from the corpse of a well developed young wcman. In the opinion of Dr. Thomson, of Oakley- square, they have been in the water about a month. Detec- tive inspectors are investigating the mystery, and have arranged to have the canal dragged for a long distance. Little doubt is felt that a murder has been committed. Srionkrao MunDER Is LONDON —The adjourned in- quest on the body of !Karam Angel, the Jewess found dead under extraordinary circumstances in the room at White- chapel, was resutned on Friday. The purchase of vitriol by the prisoner Lipski, on the morning of the murder, was clearly proved. Other witnesses deposed to Lipeki's sus- picious movements about the sane time, and medical evi- dence went to show that the unfortunate woman had first been outraged when semi-unconscieus, and then murdered. The Coroner having summed up. the jury, without any hesitation, returned, a verdict of wilful murder against Lipski. Er.xertorr Nxws.—Mr Shackleton and the Hon C Parsons have issued addresses as Conservative candidates fur the vacancy in Dublin University caused by the appointment of Mr Holmes to a judgeship. Warrants have been re- ceived appointing Mr Gibson Attorney General, and Serjeant O'Brien Solicitor General for Ireland. Poilit:l4 for the Spalding Division, for the vacancy caused by the succession of Mr. Finch Hatton (C) to the peerage, was taken on Friday, the result being expected to be declared alsout mid-day to-day. Admiral Tryon, the Conservative, and Mr. Stewart, the Gladstonian Liberal candidate, made a tour throughout the division, and were wan naly cheered by their respective supporters.
BOLTON ENGINEERS' STRIKE.-RIOTING, AND
MILITARY CALLED our.

There are 1,500 skilled' wOrkinen on strike, and only a few hands have been obtained to take their places. The crowds in the streets are in full sympathy with I those on strike, and if any of the importa- tions appeared in the streets, they would re- ceive a rough reception. The riots at Bolton, consequent upon the engineers' strike, were resumed on Thursday night, with intensity. At five o'clock the ordinary hands were leaving Meatus. Dobson and Barlow's works when the mob made a determined attempt to enter the building. This the police resisted, and then the riot commenced in earnest. Volleys of stones, brickbats, iron balls, and other missiles were thrown at the police, and no fewer than six police officers were injured, five being borough and one a county man. Police-inspector Davies was terribly injured about the head and face, and one arm Was broken. A special meeting of the magistrates was summoned, and the military telegraphed for from Manchester. The greatest excitement prevailed. The military were greeted with showere of stones, and more windows were smashed. On Friday morning the Mayor issued a proclamation calling upon the law-abiding citizens to remain at home during the disturbances, and thus assist the magistrates, who are determined to use the full power of the law in keeping down disorder. The most successful regatta ever held at Henley concluded last evening. SHOCKING IRONWORKS Exotosiox.—Shortly before nine O'clock on Friday morning, a serious explosion occurred at the Congreaves Ironworks, Cradlev Heath, belonging to the new British Iron Company, and resulted in three men being seriously, if not fatally, injured. Whilst a number of men were engaged at work at a blast furnace, a tuyere suddenly exploded, which scattered the molten metal and water amongst the workmen. The tuyere was completely shat- tered.

The House met at tour o'clock.

Several bills were advanced, and on the motion to consider the report of amendments on the Irish Land Bill, Earl DUNRAVEN said the bill had been recast and was still very nnsatistactory.—EArl SPENC6R, with every desire to see a bill passed, could only condemn the bill in the present shape, and hoped the Government wonld reconsider the provisions aff,cting leaseholders and impecunious tenants!. —Lord lisesamt and Eon COWPRR agreed that the bill pleased no one.— the Marquis of SALISBURY said if judicial tents were constantly changed confidence and capital would entirely disappear from Ireland and the evils of instability increase. The bill WAS only a temporary one, broneht forward by the Government to bring about better feeling be- tween all classes of the community in Ireland.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY adversely criticised the bill.—Earl NOWTHRELO3I( pointed out how the hill mieht be amended. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock.

_ ‘..• • • - - - QUESTIONS —The HOME SECRETARY, replying to Sir W. Lawson, said it was intended to recognise the service of the police at the Jubilee thanksgiving by awarding them a day's pay and a kronze medal —The LORD ADVOCATE, re- plying to Mr. E. Robertson, said it was intended to proceed with the Scotch Universities Bill this sessioni—Mr. A. BAD- FOUR, replying to Mr. John Morley, said if tile Irish Bill was not in the hands of members on Monday, Stipply would be taken on Tuesday. Tun Lams Qtrasprotr.—On the motion to go into Com- mittee of.. Supply, Mr. BEADLAUGH, ae an amendment, moved a resolution stating it to be the opinion of the House that the ownership of land should carry with it the duty of , cultivation and that where land was so misused and held I waste the local authorities ought to have power to acquire It compulsorily. His resolution also provided for the pay- ment of the land for a limited term by an annual sum not exceeding the then net annual produce of the land, in order that the local authorities might in their discretion let such lands to tenant cultivators. He said there I were twelve million of acres of uncultivated land in this country which ' could easily be ' ;made to to give food and employment to thousands of men now un- employed —Mr. E. STANHOPE seconded the resolution, and said it would be accepted by the country if it was rejected by that lionse --Mr H. CHAPLIN denied that men who culti- vated land in that country were arbitrarily deprived of the fruits of their labour.—Mr. W. LONG, speaking on the part of th,, Government, admitted there might be cases where I labourers wanting allotments were unable to get them, but he unhesitatingly affirmed that in nine cases out of ten' where they wanted them they could'get them.—Dr. Cranxtt supported the resolution, knowing that large landowners would rather turn the land into deer forests than allow the labourers to cultivate it.—The resolution, after considerable discussion, was rejected by 173 to 97. . RULES AND ASSESSMENTS.—Mr. CONYBEARE called at- tention to the present mode of assessment for local rates of mansions, demesnes, and parks in rural sanitary districts, and condemned the principle on which it was based as radi- cally unsound and anja9t. Wealthy owners of mansions and parks evaded their just share of local burdens which, herefore, fell in increased weight upon the farmers and tshopkeepers.

WIDNES NEW PUBLIC OFFICES, INAUGURAL DINER.

Although Widnes Local Board took poecteesion of their new paella offices in Victoe.ia-square several weeks ago, the building was not formally opened until Thursday evening. About fg. months have been occupied in the construction of the building, which, including the finishing, has. cost about £7,000. It was the original intention of the Board to erect at the same time a town hag, and plans were invited for public- offices and a town ball com- bined. To+ stimulate the architects to put forth the best efforts of their genius, the Board offered three prizes of £lOO, £3O, and .£2O, and the result was very gratifying,. as there were no less than 17 com- petitors. Many of the designs were of exceptional merit, and altimately the first' prize was awarded to Messrs. F. and G. Holme, of Liverpool, whose plans were accepted. The second prize was gained b3rMr. 'H. Shelmerdine, of Liverpool and the third by Mr. Cundall, of Leamington. The estimated cost offthe Town Hall and Public Offices was £15,000. The great depression' of trade, and the heavy burden the rates were to tradesmen and property owners, in- duced the Board subsequently to' dbfer the erection of the town halt to a more convenient period. The. need of public offices, however, was immediate and' the contract for that portion of the' building was given to Colonel Rothwell, of St. Helene. Mr. John Sadler was appointed clerk of works.. The work has been accomplished in a satisfactory and; expeditious manner, and the ratepayers now possess a building which is a permanent and striking feature in what promises to. be the centre of the business part of the town. The building is of grey bricks, but terra* cotta, a Material which best withstands the corroding inflnences of the Widnes atmos- phere, is very largely used in its conetruction. The main entrance is formed by a porch projecting from the basement of a tower, which, however, will not be conetrunted until the town hell is built. It is 19'feet high, 14 feet wide, and 4 feet 3 inches deep. Over the porch is an ornamental bal- cony of terra cotta,,with a ferocious griffin fix cdt en either side ; and below, over the porch, is the coat of arms of the town. Beautiful and finished. appearance is given to the building by the rich adornment with terracotta of all the windows. The interior is quite in. accord with the handsome appearance of the exterior. The entrance hall, a fine lofty chamber, is embellished with a dadoof green Doalton tiles, relieved with purple, and an ornamental border of redecreen, and brown tiles. Along the corridor, on the ground floor, going across to the various offices, there is a similar dado in green and blue, with a very pretty ornamental border. This corridor is 67 feet 6 inches long, and 7 feet flinches wide. To the left of the main entrance is the private office of the clerk to the Local Board, 16*feet by 17 feet 6 inches; a general office, 23 feet 6 inches by 16 feet; collector's office, 18 feet 10 inches by 14 feet;' and the nuisance in- spector's office, 13 feet 6 inches.. On the right of the entrance are the offices of the School Beard, who are the tenants of the Local Board. The private, room of the clerk is 17 feet 6 inches by 16 feet; general office, 17 feet by 2/ feet, including a strong room 5 ft. 6'in. square, inside mea- surement. and insvctor's office, 18' ft. 10 In. by 14 feet. There is alsci a committee room 22 feet wide by 15 feet, and a waiting room 22 feet by 16 feet 6.inches. Persons sum- moned before the District Education Committee will enter the waiting room from Market-street, and there is an elabo• rate arrangement of doors so that the interviews can take place expeditiously and without bustle. Behind are the caretaker's sitting room, kitchen, scullery,. lavatory, and fire engine room. In the basement also. is a strong room for the Local Board, 16 feet be 15 feet. On the first floor is the Beard-room, which is 42. feet clinches by 22 feet 5 inches with an extra bay at one end. This is a lefty and handsome chamber' well suited for the:purpose for which it is intended. It has a moulded ceiling, and running round the room to a height of four feet is a beautiful wains- cetting of old oak, with panels of walnut. At each end of the reom is a firograte and rnentlepiece made of Doulton ware, green being the prevailing colour. The table at pre- sent in use is the one that did duty at Alforde Chambers. but it is intended to fill the room up with a table of the horse-shoe pattern. The room is extremely well lighted On the first floor, too, are two commodious Local Board committee rooms, and there is also a charming little ante-room, giving entrance to the balcony, which will serve a very useful purpose at election times and other public occasions. Ou.the left are the various roomy and convenient offices of the serveyor, who is also provided with a capital strong room, 7ft On. by 15ft. Bin. A very handsome corrider gives access to the various rooms on the first floor as on the lower level. In each office is fixed a fire grate of Doulton ware, the offices ef the bead officials having, however, a fine mantelpiece of walnut. The light throughout the entire building is ex- cellent. It should be stated that the corridor on the ground floor is laid in mosaic, whilst the rooms are hid with solid wood blocks, forming a practically noiseless. floor. The upper rooms are laid with pitchpine. The corridors are fireproof. The whole arrangements of the building are highly setisfactory, and will greatly conduce to the de- spatch of public business. On Thureday evening, at the invitatioh of Mr. F. H. Goesage, J.P., the chairman of the Local Board, Ins members ef that body, and the members of the School Board, together with the head officials, were entertainee to dinner in the Board-room. Mr. Grossage previously held a reception in one of the committee-rooms. At dinner Mr. Goesece took the head of the table. the Rev. Fattier Clarke occnpying a seat at his right hand and Mr. Perrin, of Liver- pool. a seat at his left band. The vice-chair was occupied by Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., who was supported on the right by the Rev. Geo. Bond, M.A., vicar of Faro worth, and on the left by Mr. H. Gaskell, junr., J.P. There were also present Messrs. H. W. Deacon, T. Handley, R. Cook. F. Timmie. J. Midwood, D. Wright, E. Carey, B. H. Davis, B. Brown, J. B. Inflame 8, Sadler. W. W. Goseage, Captain Waring, Dr. O'Keeffe, F. Efeyes, J. Taylor, W. T. Husband, E Gossage, J. Houghton, Dr. Cooper (medical officer), J. T. Allen (clerk to Local Board), G. H. Denby (clerk to School Board). W. kligginson (surveyor), 3. Dickson (in- spector), and S. Hoyle (assistant clerk.) Dean Finegan, Mr. Bradshaw, and Mr. F. Holme (the architect) were in- vited, but Were unable to be present. The re- past had been peepared by the Cuisine Depart- ment of the Reform Club, Liverpool, and was of a most elaborate description. The following is the menu :—Hors d'oeuvres: Croute an Caviare. Soup: Clear mock turtle. Fish : Fillet of sole a l'Orly, boiled salmon, parsley saner., and cucumber. Entrees: Cutlets of chicken en supreme,Bordeaux pigeons dressed ala financier. Re- move : Boiled fowl with cream sauce, York ham. Roast : Lamb and mint sauce. Vegetables: New potatoes, spinach with cream sauce, haricot beans. Leveret with port wine sauce, asparagus and melted butter, salad ala Rinse. En- tremente : Reform pudding, fruit jellv, chocolate cresol. Savory: Cheese strawe. Dessert. The wine list comprised cl wet (Margaux), hock (Oppenheirn), sherry, port, cham- pagne, Moet's white dry Clay. The pleasureof the guests was much enhanced by the following selectiens of music, performed by the Widnes Soap Works brass hand in an ad- joining room :—March, "England's Queen," J. Frost ; over- tare," Neptune," H. Round; grand selection, a William Tell," Rorsini ; valee, "The don." R. Welch; selection. "The Bohemian girl," Belle; fantasia." Pride of Scolland," H. Round; march, " Fneland is England still," G. A. Froet ;" God save the Queen." -

Before proceeding with the toast list, Mr. Gossage ex- pressed his sincere regret at the absence of those gentlemen who, through being out of town, were unable to he present. The Chairman then gave the toast " The Queen, the Prince of Wales, and the rest of the Royal Family," in appropriate terms, and it was acknowledged with musical honours
The Chairman asked the guests to drink with equal cor- diality to "The clergy of all denominations," which was done.

The Rev. George Bond responded. They had had a most sumptuous repast, and they bad all enjoyed themselves, and he only hoped Mr. Gossage would appreciate the w-iv in which his hospitality had been received. He wished Mr Go.sage many happy returns of 'the dav—(apnlause)—a.d boned that ethers might he led to follow the example which be had set. (Laughter and applause.) The R.v. Father Clarke also responded to the toast, thanking those present for the flattering mtnner in which it had been received.

The Chairman next proposed 'The Army, Navy, and Volunteers" in a capital speech. Referring to the 'volun- teers, he said our great army of citizen soldiers was the greatest example that had ever been put before the world of the resources of this netion, and the manner in which from year to year they had increased in numbers and efficiency have commanded the respect of the whole world. (Ap- plause.) fie trusted the volunteers would become more efficient and more numerous, but his greatest prayer was that they might never have to fire a shot in defence of this country. (AePlatiFe.) The toast having been honoured, Captain Wareing responded. He said the valour, the. sacrifice, and the heroism of the twin forces were matters of history, and known to them all—(hear, hear)—and he might eifely say that itteneyer and wherever these forces might be called in active service they would be found not only ready and willing, but able to sustain the glorious tra- ditioas that were already written on the scroll of fame. (Apolmse.) With regard to the volunteers, with which he had the honour to be intimately connected, they could not boast of any military achievements, but what they could , and did boast or was a patriotism that was at once the envy I and admiration of the civilized world—(hear, hear)—and if I ever the time did come, God forbid that it ever would, they would be found ready, willing, and able to perform the duty that would be assigned to them of protecting their hearths and homer. (Applause). Mr. Brown give the toast The magistrates," and after a humorous reference to his appearance before the bench. mentioned the antiquity of the office, and the important functions pertaining to it. and went on to say that in Wid- nes they were blessed with no ordinary men as magistrates. and hew they could afford to give day after day their time , and careful attention to the work he could not tell. It was to services like these, given willingly, faithfully, and gratu- itously for the common welfare that Englaud owed her 1 security., Since there had been an adeli,ion to the local 1 magistrates he thought that the order of the town had been ceneiderably increased from some reason or other, He thought there was an influence ererted amongst the popu- lation, and hoped that it would continue until they had in Widnes as loyal and law-abiding a population as any other town. (Applause). The toast, which was coupled with the name of Mr, IL Gaskell, junr, was heartily honoured.

lln respondjng, Mr Gaskell saiel the duties of magistrates were sometimes rather arduous and at other times extremely niipleasant. 4Hear, hear.) It was very gratifying to the magistrates to think that the performance of those duties had met with the approval of the townspeople. Of course there WJP a certain section of the town:from whom they could hardly hope or expect approval. They would have recently fanned that Widnee was DOW being made into a separate polite dietriCt. (applause) This was a matter of consi- derable importance to the town. He was sure that whenever opportunity offered, the- maaistrates of that district would always be found to the fore in any undertaking which would add to. the importance and wefflare of Widnes. (Applause.) Dr. ID'lCeeffe submitted the tract of "The town aid trado of Widnes," and in a lengthy speech be mentioned the fact that the Manor of Widnes was formed in the daye of Vrellieru the Conqueror, and was entered in Domesday Book. Be ' wont on to say that 40 or SO years ago Widnes proper con- ' slated of a few farmhouse and a few labourers cottages; and' 22 years ago, when he came to Widnes' the " Snig Pie Hone° " Was a truly mod residence. (Learghter and ap- plause.) In the year 1850 a new industry, foe Widnes at all evente, was brought there by the resources of gentlemen of science and ability who made use of their beano for the benefit of humanity. (Applause), He mentioned the late Mr. Goesage as Oar, pioneer of the chemittal tractbe and said from hinatreat faulty of invention, from his perseverance and from his skill, he wee a powerful mane and wee one of the great means of making Widnes what it was that day. (Apoleusee) He also mentioned' Mn John Hutchinson, Mr. nicLellanea and last, though not least, the late Mr. Henry , ,Deacon—(ceplause)--who was a man of great enterprise and energy. He hoped thatthe new people who were corn- kg into the town would act as the old manufacturers. bad ' done—(hear.. hear,) —and that they would do all in their power for the prosperity of the town and trade of Wilma& Pifty years act the population was only about 900; but now it was estimated at 30,000, but he thought a more accnrate figxre would be 33,000. He thought this state of things was entirely owing to the excellent sanitary work that was carried on by the members of the Local Board under the able presidency of their chairman. (Hear, hear.) Benno conaleading he would like to refer to the vend open epacee they had in the town;. they were so many lungs for the people. (Hear, hear.) Tha surveyor also deserved a word of praise for the admirable roads he had made in the town- ship,and on several occasions the inspectors of the Local Government Board had gone out of their way to compli- ment him upon them.. (Applause.) The toast having been honoured, Mr H. Wade Deacon re- plied. 16 one sense, he said, he felt that it was suitable that he should reply te this toast, because he was rapidly be- coming one of the oldest inhabitants of Widnes. (Hear, hear.) Anyone jndging from the external aspect of the place would come, and did come' to the conclusion that it was a ' miserable hole," and that the inhabitants were wicked and miserable also. But what were the facts. Thor were undoubtedly a working population, some of them with their headerhnt inset of thorn with their hands, and. they were trying to get money, or not te lose what they bad made. In such a population there must be a certain rough element, but he thought it nal creditable, and a matter of great congratulation to the town, that serious crime was an extremely rare occurrence in Widnes. (Applause.) Then they had a very good supply of places of worship of various denomicarioce, and the various sects lived in friendly rela- tions with one another. (epplause.), They had a most excellent stipply of public elementary schools. (Applause.) They had a Grammar School, which would no doubt do much good in, the future. They had a most excellent Science and Art School, which had been in existence for ten or eleven years, of' which Mr. Gossage was president, and now they bad what would prove of the utmost benefit to the inhabitants—a Free Library. (Hear, hear.) This was an institution that he was certain would leave its mark. Mr. Deacon referred to the means cf recreation in existence in the town, and he concluded from what he had mentioned that there was a s'rong nubile opinion in the town in favour of all that was noble and true, and opposed to all that was degrading and evil. (Applause.) So long as they had this feeling amongst the people, they would progresses a town, and be a credit to their forefathers. There was one Point mentioned by Mr. Bond with which he agreed very much. 't hey had been somewhat deficient in civic social life, and he congratulated their chairman upon giving this occasion for a social meeting of the two popu- larly elected Boards of the town. (Applause.) They should not always have dinners like that.; they did not ex- pect it, but he did trust that now they had these public offices they would have gentlemen following the example that had been set that night, and that opportunities will be seized of having social gatherings of the townspeople of Widnes. (Applause) Speaking as a manufacturer, he would say that the staple industry of Wid- nes had been for a long time under a cloud. There had been a world wide depres- sion in the alkali trade, and Widnes had had an es- pecial blow struck at it. It was therefore a matter for satis- faction that there were fresh industries. being introduced into the town and neighbourhood—(applause)—and that new works were being erected. They had suffered in Wid- 1 nes from the depression in trade, but it was a matter of thankfulness that there had not bees that terrible amount of destitution amongst the population that had been seen in other towns. (Applause.) Mr. Deacon alluded to the fact that strikes were almost unknown in the town,and concluded by giving a history of the Traders' Association, in which he described the important part the gentlemen connected with it bad had in the development of the town. Mr. Sadler also mad* an appropriate- response to The toamt.

Mr: It. H. Davies next proposed "Widnes Local Board." The ratepayers and the inhabitants generally were, be said, greatly indebted to the Local Board for the good work they had done amongst them; The Board was formed in the year 1885 i and at that time the gas supply and the water supply was in the hands of a limited liability company. Shortly afterwards the Board obtained Parliamentary powers to purchase these works, and the town had now a inagnificient supply of very good water. In 1878 the Market was established, in 1878, the Accident Hospital was established, and in 1887 they had the Library opened, and to crown :he edifice they had that .beantiful building in which they were assembled. (Applause'.) The toast was drunk with enthusiasm.

The Chairman responded, and said that the advantages offered by the place, induced his father to come, a poor man, to try and establish a business that had not yet been de- veloped. The railway to Garston and Warrington, be men- tioned. was opened in 1853, and at that time there was no Local Board, no gas, and no water supply. He thought he had a right to speak for the Local Board, for if he were spared to finish his present term of office, be wofild have served—he hoped faithfully—the ratepayers for a continu- ity of twenty years. (Applause.) Mr. Gossage gave some reminiscences of his connection with the Board, and went on to say that in 1853, when he first came to Widnes, he did ' not believe that in Widnes proper there were 600 inhabitants land now the population hart Increased to nearly. 33,000; a rate of 'progress that was remarkable even in modern times, (Hear, hear.) As to water, he believed they were In a posi- tion to supply even Liverpool at a price which tho Corpora- tion of that city could not do itself, and which would leave Widnes a profit. (Hear, bear.) The Board, through the labours of Mr. Gaskell, jour., and the Water Committee, would soon be able to reduce the price of water to some- ' thing below sd. (Applause.) He then thanked the mem- ' hers for the extreme courtesy which they had always shown 'towards him, and for the manner in which they had always- received his ruling. Mr. Carey, in proposing the toast of "The School Eoard," I coupled with the name of Mr. Timmis, said that the ele- mentary education of Widnes should be conducted with the utmost possible economy combined with efficiency. He thought that the Board had been economical and efficient, and that they had acted in the most fair way, so far as the law would allow them, towards denominational schools in the township. Theoretically the Board and denominational schools were treated alike, but they all knew that in many cases there was a cruel injustice done to the denominational schools. (Hear, hear.) He thought they might congra- tulate the School Board at Widnes on the success of the past. He then proposed "Health, prosperity, and long life ' to the Chairman." (Applause.) After the enthusiasm which had been invoked had subsided _

Mr. Timmis replied. He gave a number of figures show- ing the progress that bad been made in elementary educa• tion since the formation of the School Board in 1874. The population was then 15,000, and the number of children in attendance at voluntary schools was 1,521. The number of children at present attending voluntary schools was 31C03 and in board schools 3,131; so ttat there was a total in- crease of 200 per cent. The present School Board rate was ap, and the average rate since the Board was farmed was sd. As to Government grint, the sum received in 188G•in Widnes Board Schools was 12e) 2,11 per head, and the aver- nee throughout the United Kingdon was 17s 7id. (Ap- plAnse.) Mr. Handley proposed the toast of "The officials of the Local Board and School Board," coupled with the names of Dr. Cooper Mr. Allen, and Mr. Danby. These gentle- men responded, and then the sentiment, "The Chairman, Mrs Gossage, and family," was given with enthusiast!), on the preposition of Mr. D, Wright. The company sang: with much heartiness " For they are jolly good foellows. In conclusion the Chairman proposed "The Ladies," which was responded to by Mr. F. Heyes •, and than" The Press," which was replied to by Mr.'Whslley, of this journal.
AN EVICTION SCENE AT WIDNES.

Yesterday morning Mr. Barnett Dutton, auctioneer. Oak- land-street, accompanied by Frederick Wilson, rent bailiff, and another bailiff from Manchester, went to the house of a labourer named Callighan, in, Alforde-street, for the purpose of making a distraint for rent. Whllst Mr. Dutton and his assistants were endeavouring to gain admittance Mrs Callihan, from an upper room window emptied a kettle full of boiling water upon Mr. Dutton, who was moat severely scalded about the face and neck. The woman then threw tl4 kettle through the window, and the ugly missle alighted on ?he head of Wilson, and smashed into fragments. Wil- son was very seriously injured. The other bailiff was also slightly scalded, and P.S. McGregor, who was present for the purpose of preventing a breach of the peace, was also assaulted, but not seriously. Both Mt. Dutton and Wilson were Sal a dangerous condition, and although the woman is in custody, and will be brought before the magistrates to- day (Saturday), it is probable that Inspector Keighley will ask for a remand.

The yards of the shops in High-street were invadcd by the molten tallest and , resin, and the floor of the bakehouse of Mr. 11. Gorst, fectioner, was covered to a &gab of /8 inches; but laes4, the damage done was of a comparatively trifling nature. .1,-% loss sustained by Messrs. Hazleleurst through the destruot,rv, of so much valuable material is very heavy, but we anus stand ie covered by insurance. Two accidents occurred de 'ing the exciting &Mir. John Ainee, of 79, Nelsotest!!„,s. e,i 'whilst directing a stream of water front a high wail be°l .Mrs. Poole's shop, fell to the ground, and severely loidre,,,, himself. His ankle Was sprained, his back and legs-v/19o . badly hurt, and he was generally shaken.
